item.title: 2 reasons why the Raiders might give the 49ers fits
item.description: We look at a couple of different ways the Raiders can make the 49ers life a little tougher on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers used their bye week wisely, shoring up the defensive line by adding DeForest Buckner.

The 49ers have one final game before the trade deadline, hosting their former neighbors, the Las Vegas Raiders. With San Francisco getting a bye week following its first loss of the season, the Raiders ended a four-game skid with a win over the Jets.

Las Vegas started hot with a 3-0 start, but that quickly turned to 3-4 before the Week 8 win. The 49ers look to return the Raiders to their losing ways on Sunday.

Here are three numbers to know going into the former Battle of the Bay:

1

Team. The Raiders are the only team in the league to be in the bottom three in yards allowed and points allowed. 

Simply put: the Raiders’ defense is bad. It’s 381.9 yards allowed per game, the third-most allowed (only the Titans and Cowboys are worse), and the 28.8 points allowed per game is second-worst (only Arizona has allowed more, and the Colts are slightly better). 

And the scary thing for Vegas is the defense is only getting worse. In each of its last five games, the Raiders have allowed 30 or more points after allowing just 27 points combined in the first two games of the season. Part of the reason the points have gone up is the Raiders just can’t stop the ball.

Las Vegas has allowed more than its average of 382 yards in four of the last five games, with the offense only able to keep up last week, going 1-4 in those five games.

The New York Jets scored 30 points for the first time since Week 8 of last season. It’s easy to see a 49ers offense even without Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel putting up points against this Raiders defense. 

13

Turnovers. The Raiders defense has forced 13 turnovers, fifth-most in the league. 

Not a good one, but a defense that can take the ball away if you aren’t careful, and the 49ers haven’t been protective of the ball recently. Hopefully the bye week fixed that issue.

The Raiders have been plenty opportunistic (and maybe a little lucky) with only five interceptions, placing them in the middle of the league in picking the ball off. Where the Raiders shine is when the ball is loose, with seven fumble recoveries. The bad news: the 49ers average a fumble per game, with five of the six that were lost coming in San Francisco’s last three games.

Turnovers have been a recent plague for the 49ers. After turning the ball over two times in the first four games, San Francisco has eight turnovers in the last three games, with four of those coming against an Atlanta team that entered Week 7 with just six turnovers. 

The Raiders defense can be beat, but the 49ers must shake this recent turnover issue to fully take advantage. 

265.1

Passing yards per game. The Raiders offense averages 265.1 passing yards per game, third-best in the league.

While the Raiders defense isn’t great, its offense is explosive, which puts them in the category of “not a great team, but a fun team” that has the ability to get into a shootout. In four of the Raiders’ eight games this season, both teams have scored more than 24 points, with the Raiders splitting those games. 

The spark for the Las Vegas offense has been giving second-year tight end Brock Bowers a competent quarterback in veteran Kirk Cousins. Cousins has turned the clock back with Las Vegas under Klint Kubiak, throwing for 19 touchdowns and five interceptions through the first half of the season. His 6.7 touchdown percentage is his highest since 2020, while his 1.8 interception rate is his lowest since 2023.

But Bowers has been the key to Cousins’ resurgence. Despite missing the first two games of the season, the tight end leads the Raiders in targets by 14, receptions by four, receiving yards by 73, and touchdowns by one. The Las Vegas offense looked fine in the two games without Bowers but has taken a step up with him, scoring 30 points in three of the six games the tight end has played in.

How the 49ers choose to cover Bowers will be something to watch. They could use a safety (maybe Ji’Ayir Brown?) or maybe a corner (but the 49ers’ corners might have a tough time with the size of Bowers). I’m curious to see if the 49ers even throw Fred Warner at Bowers a few times just to see how he handles it.

item.title: LSU Football’s NFL Draft Stock: First-round landing spots
item.description: Where could Jordan Seaton and Trey’Dez Green land?
item.content:encoded:
With LSU just coming off their bye week, the draft stock around the team really didn’t change, so I wanted to focus on landing spots for the Tigers projected to be selected in the first round instead.

LT Jordan Seaton

One of, if not the, most important players on LSU’s roster, Jordan Seaton is bound for the top of the 2027 NFL Draft. With his athleticism and impact in both run and pass protection, Seaton will be coveted by most of the teams in the NFL. LT is one of the most important positions in football, and many teams do not have that franchise guy that they won’t have to worry about for a decade. Seaton can be that player.

Looking at the teams that could be in for Seaton, I’ll just focus on the top-5 because that’s where he is likely going. After Texas tackle Trevor Goosby’s injury, Seaton is the lone tackle at the top of the class (for now). As of this week, the top 5 of the draft is 1. Los Angeles Chargers, 2. Tennessee Titans, 3. Miami Dolphins, 4. New York Jets, and 5. Philidelphia Eagles.

Starting with the Chargers, they are likely going to go in a different direction because tackle is not their biggest need and WR Jeremiah Smith is by far the top player in the draft. The Titans on the other hand do need an upgrade at tackle, and if they view Seaton as the second best player in the class, they will likely take him. After Tennessee, all three of the Dolphins, Jets, and Eagles can go for Seaton, but the Dolphins and Jets have needs at QB, which will over rule selecting the offensive tackle.

TE Trey’Dez Green

Unlike Seaton, Trey’Dez Green is not a top-10 lock just yet, and he is rivaled by another TE in the class. Oregon’s Jamari Johnson is also incredible and will consisdred the top TE in the class, but Green’s athleticsm may be the difference maker. Some of the plays he is able to make is truly incredible, and any team could covet him for their offense.

When trying to find potential suitors, three teams stand out: Seattle Seahawks, New England Patriots, and Kansas City Chiefs. For the Seahawks, they currently have the highest pick out of the three teams, and although that may change, adding Green to a team like this could bring them right back to the Super Bowl. Similar is true for the Patriots, and in the Chiefs case, Green could be Travis Kelce’s succesor.

item.title: Interview with the Enemy: Cleveland Browns
item.description: Chris Pokorny joins us for Week 9 of IWTE.
item.content:encoded:
This week, the New Orleans Saints will return to action to face the Cleveland Browns at Caesars Superdome in Week 9 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Chris Pokorny of Dawgs By Nature joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup.

NJ: How would you evaluate Todd Monken’s first season as the Browns’ head coach? What have been the biggest positives and negatives since his arrival in Cleveland?

CP: It certainly got off to a rocky start after the Browns were blown out with no answers in Week 1 against the Jaguars. After that, though, things have been much better, to the point where he was getting coach of the year recognition (prior to the second blowout loss against Pittsburgh last week). I wouldn’t say he’s an amazing coach, but he’s gotten some good out of Deshaun Watson, which not many people thought was possible. As a team in general, and this extends to defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg too, the thing I’ve liked the most is that we’ve seen some week-to-week and in-game adjustments, which is something the previous coaching staff didn’t do well.

In terms of negatives, there are a few things that Monken hasn’t been able to figure out: how to prevent Watson from getting sacked at a near-record pace, and how to cut out the high number of penalties. I don’t know if either of those is really an indictment on Monken, though, especially since the offensive line has played at what I would call a fair level this season. Cleveland has also had the benefit of an ‘easy schedule,’ so I’d give him like a B- so far in his first year as a head coach.

NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Browns on Sunday against the Saints? Is there a particular area in which New Orleans could exploit?

CP: Obviously, it’s looking like Deshaun Watson will be out as he is in the concussion protocol. All things considered, though, Cleveland has been relatively healthy this season. The player I might look at is second-year linebacker Carson Schwesinger. He is the type of player who could be a future All-Pro, and has had games where he lights it up. But, he also has a warrior mentality to where he’ll play through injuries. He’s been dealing with an ankle injury, and while it didn’t seem to hinder him previously, last week against the Steelers, he had an awful day in coverage, grading out as a 30.5 by Pro Football Focus. He had low marks across the board,
 grading poorly in run defense, tackling, pass rush, and coverage.

It’s possible that was an anomaly, and that targeting Schwesinger might actually be a mistake, given his overall body of work. But it’s worth pointing out, given what happened last week. If we’re not talking about injuries, the area the Saints should try to explore is the Browns’ run defense. It has become a real liability lately, with the Titans and Steelers shredding it and the Browns not having any answers. Cleveland’s coaching staff talked about what went wrong this past week from a strategic standpoint against the run, so we’re hoping to see adjustments. But Cleveland’s pass defense is very sound, so the Saints — despite their struggles on the ground — are far better suited trying to capitalize on what’s worked for others lately via the ground game.

NJ: With Shedeur Sanders in line to start on Sunday in New Orleans, how confident are you in his ability to operate the offense and rally his teammates?

CP: Deshaun Watson has looked way better this season than he has in previous seasons with the Browns, and his knack for leading a game-winning drive — he’s done it in all five victories — can’t be denied. With that said, though, he’s still been a below average quarterback in my book because things are generally still a bit slow to process. At times, he seems timid to make a mistake downfield, which is both a good and bad thing. Worst of all is the inconsistency, though. Most weeks, it seems like the offense goes cold for three of the game’s four quarters, before finding a spark in one of the quarters. There isn’t a consistent rhythm. That’s not all on Watson, but I think a lot of it is.

My point in mentioning all of that is that, despite Watson’s 5-3 record, I can’t really see it being ‘worse’ for Shedeur Sanders, per se. I mean, Watson hasn’t thrown a touchdown pass in three straight games. Last year, we saw a mix of good and bad for Sanders, but that also came behind a much worse offensive line in my opinion. I’m intrigued to see how Sanders plays with the Browns’ young weapons this year. One of Sanders’ biggest issues in the past has been backpedaling too much on third downs to try to avoid pressure, and it just leads to a bigger sack. He got better at it during the regular season last year, but because it’s been so long since he’s faced live game action, it’s possible that those tendencies will creep up again. Back in training camp, I thought he flashed some good chemistry with rookie WR KC Concepcion when they got reps together, which is a plus. Overall, I have like an average level of confidence that he’ll operate the offense fine. I don’t know about rallying his teammates. I’m not expecting a Gardner Minshew moment where he comes in and leads touchdown drives left and right, but I’m expecting him to keep us in the game at least as much as Watson would have.

NJ: Who is one Browns player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance?

CP: I’ll go with tight end Harold Fannin. After a little lull where he only had 2 catches in 2 games, he’s had 16 catches for 245 yards in the last 2 games. He catches the ball well, and always has a knack for gaining an extra few yards after contact, no matter which defender is tackling him. In 7 games with Sanders last year at quarterback, Fannin had 4 touchdown receptions and a fair amount of targets week-to-week, so I’m expecting some of that hookup to continue this week.

NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook, the Saints (-164) are currently 3.0-point favorites over the Browns (+138) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction and how do you see the game playing out?

CP: It looks like the line shifted to +3, possibly with the news of Watson being in the concussion protocol. This is the end of a three-game road stretch for Cleveland, and they’re coming off of a bad loss. Also, in the Browns’ five victories this season, none of them have been by more than 4 points. On paper, I tell myself that Cleveland’s offense will find some success, since the Saints are allowing nearly 28 points per game. Although the Browns’ run defense has suffered lately, I think it’ll be a point of emphasis in the film room this week, and New Orleans has not had a lot of success in that area. If New Orleans stays one-dimensional, Cleveland is tough to pass the ball on consistently, so I see the potential for this week’s game being advantageous to the Browns. I’ll go with the Browns coming out on top 20-17.

Thank you again to Chris Pokorny for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here.

item.title: Cowboys vs. Colts recent history puts spotlight on coaching
item.description: The Cowboys recent history with the Colts is mixed
item.content:encoded:
The Dallas Cowboys visit the Indianapolis Colts for the first time since 2018 this Sunday, and have played their way into a corner where this is an unfortunate bad versus bad game. Brian Schottenheimer’s Cowboys are yet again continuing their pattern of mostly alternating wins and losses, and only having losing streaks compared to winning streaks, into November. They go to Indy with a 3-5 record, off a 33-30 overtime loss at home to the Cardinals. The Colts are off yet another loss at the Jaguars, but it marked their fourth straight to sit at 2-6 right now.

The Colts have already accepted this 2026 campaign as a lost season, trading away players like Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner for future assets, with more personnel and coaching changes expected for a season that’s failed to match even mild-ish expectations. The Cowboys have done no such thing, teasing the possibility of actually being buyers in the trade market still with the awfulness of the NFC East adding fuel to this fire.

There’s also been nothing but votes of confidence in the coaching staff, which again may be a two-fold result of still having a “winnable” division, as well as not having an obvious answer to who would replace Schottenheimer in-season if a change was made, nor Klayton Adams or Christian Parker.

If the Cowboys want to continue selling any semblance of hope for this season, beating a team that’s already punted on that hope is obviously a must. Yes, we mostly said the same about the Cardinals game that was one of the worst collapses in recent memory, but at bare minimum that wasn’t an opponent that has given up. Getting in the win column in their third to last game before Thanksgiving, with another one of these also coming against a bad AFC South opponent the Titans, is the best the Cowboys can do this Sunday.

Their absolute most recent game against the Colts came in Week 13 of 2022. The Cowboys had a second-year head coach just like they do now, but it was Mike McCarthy who beat the Colts 54-19 in Dallas. It was the third straight win of four in a row, all four in response to an overtime loss at the Packers. The Cowboys also beat the Vikings 40-3 in this stretch.

The most recent away game in the series for Dallas came in 2018. The Cowboys were coming off of missing the playoffs in 2017 after Dak Prescott’s amazing rookie campaign of 2016, and patience was wearing thin for head man Jason Garrett, but more so offensive coordinator Scott Linehan. Presently, the Cowboys have these responsibilities both on Schotty’s shoulders as he is the play-calling head coach. These 2018 Cowboys were in the same position, 3-5, as the 2026 team.

They won five straight to reach 8-5 by Week 15, but then were shutout for the first time since 2003 in a 23-0 loss at the Colts. The Cowboys got into Colts territory on the opening drive of the game but had a field goal blocked, got it into the red zone the next possession but turned it over on downs, then proceeded to punt twice, turn it over on downs two more times, and end the game with an interception. Blake Jarwin had the longest catch of the game for Dallas for 18 yards.

The Colts defensive coordinator responsible for keeping the Cowboys off the scoreboard in this game? None other than Matt Eberflus, who had spent the last seven seasons as the Cowboys linebackers coach, and the 2016-17 seasons also taking on passing game coordinator duties.

Cowboys fans worst nightmares about the predictability of Linehan’s offense were realized with the harshest reality check possible, a coach that worked in the same building as Linehan the year before having all of the answers to the test and shoving the Cowboys offense in a locker for four quarters.

It is pretty wild to also consider the fact Eberflus parlayed this defensive coordinator job with the Colts into his first head coaching job with the Bears, and that was his final stop before returning to Dallas as DC to work with Schottenheimer last year.

Eberflus is also now with the San Francisco 49ers, who are tied with the Vikings and Bills for having the best record in the NFL. If the Cowboys get this weekend’s win against the Colts, that elusive winning streak will be in play only by beating Eberflus and the 49ers back at home the following week.

Today’s Cowboys almost assuredly don’t have the same luxury of being able to lose this game to the Colts and still make the playoffs as a 3-5 team that would fall to 3-6, but whether or not they’re even playoff worthy will have to remain a discussion even with a blowout win.

It is an awkward spot to be in, and the hollowness of this game feels like a direct result of coaching malpractice – the seeds of which were planted as early as the last time the Cowboys were in Indianapolis, or possibly even earlier.

It may not be far fetched at all to say both of these organizations coming into week nine have more to look forward to when they’ll be in Lucas Oil Stadium for the Combine this offseason, searching for the prospects that can turn fortunes around. The Colts have already positioned themselves to be ahead of the Cowboys (not a hard thing to do) in the offseason coaching search if they choose to do so though, as the realization of how much that matters has yet to hit Jerry Jones.

item.title: TreVeyon Henderson provides medical update, reveals recent hospitalization for ‘unexplainable’ illness
item.description: The Patriots running back has been out since last week.
item.content:encoded:
New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson, who had been out since last Thursday due to an illness, took to social media on Friday to provide an update on his medical situation.

“Recently, I experienced an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms that required hospitalization for several days,” Henderson wrote in the statement. “During that time, I underwent extensive medical testing and evaluation. While the results of my comprehensive medical testing have comeback positive and reassuring, the cause o f this remains unknown and unexplainable.”

“I will continue working closely with specialists and physical therapists to focus on my recovery, as these symptoms have affected my strength, coordination, and some of my physical functions. I am committed to doing everything necessary to return to full health. My health and long-term well-being remain my foremost priority.”

Henderson, 24, joined the Patriots as a second-round selection in the 2025 NFL Draft and burst onto the scene as a big-play threat. Serving in tandem with veteran running back Rhamondre Stevenson, he finished his rookie campaign with 1,132 scrimmage yards and 10 touchdowns.

His second NFL campaign, however, has been a challenge.

Henderson suffered an ankle injury in late August that forced him out multiple weeks into the regular season. He returned in Week 2 against the Steelers — a game that saw him score a 39-yard touchdown reminiscent of his 2025 form — but has touched the ball only 57 total times for 248 scrimmage yards and that one score since then. Along the way, he also suffered a high ankle sprain and has missed time due to his current illness.

That illness first came up last week leading up to New England’s game in Miami. Henderson was a full participant in practice on Wednesday before being absent the following two days and into the game. He was also a non-participant in practice so far this week.

The Patriots will host the Green Bay Packers at Gillette Stadium on Sunday. In light of his statement,Henderson’s participation appears to be in doubt.

item.title: Week 9 Fantasy Football Matchups to Exploit: Patriots, Dolphins have multiple players in good spots

We're into Week 9 of the fantasy football season and plenty of new names have emerged as assets. With that, we have to evaluate which players are in the best spots. That's where Ray Garvin comes in with his matchups to exploit for fantasy football in Week 9.

Jonah Coleman, RB, Broncos at Panthers

I'm buying into Jonah Coleman this week, and I think there's a real chance he finishes as an RB1 against Carolina.

Coleman got his opportunity with RJ Harvey on injured reserve and made the most of it. He handled 11 carries for 41 yards and a touchdown against Kansas City, adding four catches for 63 yards on five targets. More importantly, he out-touched J.K. Dobbins 15-7 and played nearly 68% of Denver's offensive snaps. He also ran 17 routes on 34 dropbacks. That's not just a rookie getting a few designed touches. That's a running back earning a role.

Now, he gets a Panthers defense allowing 28.3 full-PPR points per game to opposing backfields, second-most in the NFL. Carolina is surrendering 4.73 yards per carry and has already given up 10 rushing touchdowns. Since Week 4, opposing lead backs have averaged roughly 20 PPR points per game against them.

That's the part that makes this matchup so appealing. Coleman doesn't need 20 carries to beat his ranking. If he's getting double-digit rushes, involved in the passing game and seeing valuable touches near the goal line, the ceiling is there.

He's RB16 in half-PPR consensus, but I'm comfortable starting him as an RB2 with legitimate top-12 upside. I don't expect Dobbins to disappear, but this looks like Coleman's backfield to lead right now.

Rhamondre Stevenson, RB, Patriots vs. Packers

Rhamondre Stevenson is another running back I'm willing to push up my rankings, especially if TreVeyon Henderson misses another game.

With Henderson out last week, Stevenson carried the ball 19 times for 82 yards and added three receptions. The other Patriots' backs combined for nine carries. That's the type of workload we want to see, even if there wasn't a touchdown attached to it.

And I like how this matchup sets up.

Green Bay has allowed 25.0 full-PPR points per game to opposing backfields, seventh-most in the league. An opposing running back has scored at least 13 PPR points against the Packers in four straight games. That's not a defense I'm treating as a shutdown matchup for the position.

There's also a physicality element here. Stevenson has shown the ability to make defenders miss, while Green Bay has struggled to limit yards after contact recently. If New England keeps giving him opportunities, he can create something even when the initial blocking isn't perfect.

The receiving work matters, too. Stevenson has 23 catches on the season, so he isn't entirely dependent on getting into the end zone to help your lineup. He's also averaging just 3.8 yards per carry, which makes that additional volume even more important.

Henderson missed Wednesday and Thursday practices with an illness. We still need the final injury designation, but if he's out, Stevenson is a strong RB2 for me with top-12 upside. He's RB15 in consensus, and the workload could push him past that.

DeMario Douglas, WR, Patriots vs. Packers

We need to talk about DeMario Douglas, because there's an actual opportunity here if A.J. Brown misses another game.

Douglas led New England with 76 receiving yards last week, catching all three of his targets and scoring on a 48-yard touchdown. He's now scored four touchdowns over his past four games and topped 65 receiving yards in three of them.

Now, am I telling you three targets are enough to feel comfortable? Absolutely not. That's the concern. One big play carried his Week 8 production, and we can't just assume he's going to score every Sunday.

But the matchup gives us something to work with. Green Bay is allowing 34.8 full-PPR points per game to opposing wide receiver groups, ninth-most in the NFL. If Brown remains out, Douglas has a chance to operate as one of Drake Maye's primary passing-game options.

Keeping it real here, the Packers have been tougher on slot receivers than those overall numbers suggest. This isn't a free square. Green Bay has also been good at limiting explosive passes, so the targets may need to grow if Douglas is going to hit.

Still, with Brown and Hunter Henry both missing practice Wednesday and Thursday, it's reasonable to expect New England to lean on the weapons it has available.

Douglas is WR31 in half-PPR consensus. I'm comfortable with him as a flex play, especially if I need upside. Just understand that the ceiling is more attractive than the floor.

Malik Willis, QB, Dolphins vs. Lions

If you're streaming quarterbacks, Malik Willis is somebody I'm willing to take a shot on this week.

Detroit is allowing 24.8 fantasy points per game to opposing quarterbacks, the most in the NFL. And this isn't just one ugly game skewing the numbers. Every quarterback the Lions have faced has finished QB13 or better, and they've allowed multiple passing touchdowns in every game.

That's the matchup.

Now, look at Willis. He's thrown two touchdowns in each of his past two starts, including 211 passing yards against New England last week. He also has 225 rushing yards and three rushing touchdowns on the season. When the passing production and rushing production hit in the same game, he can give you a real difference-making fantasy performance.

But here's the part we can't ignore: Detroit can get after the quarterback.

The Lions are averaging 3.4 sacks per game, second-most in the league, while Miami has allowed pressure on 42.9% of dropbacks. Willis was sacked five times last week. That's a real concern and the biggest reason I'm not calling him a locked-in QB1.

Still, a quarterback who can create with his legs facing a defense that has consistently surrendered touchdowns is exactly the kind of streamer I'm interested in.

Willis is QB13 in consensus. I think he has a path to a top-10 finish, and if you're choosing between fringe starters this week, I'm leaning into the upside.

Greg Dulcich, TE, Dolphins vs. Lions

Greg Dulcich might be my favorite tight end streamer this week, and it's not just because Detroit has been awful against the position.

The usage is moving in the right direction.

Across his past three games, Dulcich has earned a 20% target share and a 25.5% first-read share while running a route on 62.6% of Miami's dropbacks. He's also averaging 2.68 yards per route run over that stretch. Those aren't empty routes. He's getting open, getting targeted and producing when the ball comes his way.

He's caught 13 passes for 166 yards in those three games without scoring a touchdown. Last week, he saw six targets and turned them into four catches for 43 yards.

Now we get to the matchup.

Detroit is allowing 27.9 full-PPR points per game to tight ends, the most in football. Through seven games, the Lions have surrendered 11 receiving touchdowns to the position. Over their past five games, they've also allowed the most receiving fantasy points per game and the third-most yards per target to tight ends.

That's exactly what I'm looking for when streaming a tight end: a player earning opportunities against a defense giving up efficiency and touchdowns at the position.

Dulcich is TE17 in half-PPR consensus. I'm willing to start him over some of the usual low-end TE1 options. I think he's got a legitimate chance to finish inside the top 12, and one touchdown could turn this into a really good week.

item.title: What the Chiefs are saying about the Jets
item.description: Kansas City’s coaching staff previewed New York at the podium this week.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 9, the Kansas City Chiefs will host the New York Jets near the midpoint of the 2026 regular season. The game at Arrowhead Stadium will feature a coaching matchup of second-year head coach Aaron Glenn and Chiefs head coach Andy Reid in his 28th season.

At the podium Wednesday, Reid looked forward to the matchup with New York by describing the team Kansas City hasn’t faced in three years. The Chiefs won a road game on “Sunday Night Football” 23-20 in Week 4 of the 2023 season.

“They’re very physical on both sides of the ball,” Reid said. “Scoring a lot of points on the offensive side, and their defense – they’ve got a lot of different looks that they’re going to present. Solid veteran players that do a nice job for them.”

Glenn, a former NFL cornerback and Detroit Lions defensive coordinator, is organizing a unit that just allowed 38 points to the Las Vegas Raiders at home last week. However, this season, New York ranks 11th in total yards allowed per game (318) and allows the fifth-lowest rate of passing yards per game (194).

“They’ve got some good veteran guys, whether it’s the safeties, the linebackers. You’re not going to have things that are botched up,” Reid shared. “They do a good job of making sure they can adjust to most things and do it accurately. Then they’ve got some guys on the front that are good football players, big guys. They’re good players. They’ve got some good speed on the outside.”

Whether it’s linebacker Demario Davis or safety Minkah Fitzpatrick, the Jets made sure to bring in veterans to lead Glenn’s group this season. Chiefs offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy pointed out the style of defense Glenn has instilled.

“They play extremely hard,” Bieniemy pointed out. “They play fast and A.G.,obviously, they haven’t had the best of luck, but when you turn that tape on, they get your attention.”

On the flip side, the Chiefs’ defense will face a hot Jets offense. They have scored 58 points over the last two weeks, and first-round rookies in wide receiver Omar Cooper Jr. and tight end Kenyon Sadiq have had big games around No. 1 wide receiver Garrett Wilson.

With Wilson in concussion protocol this week, Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo is still ready to defend downfield passes from veteran quarterback Geno Smith, who was once his quarterback when he was defensive coordinator and interim head coach of the New York Giants in 2017.

Smith was also the quarterback for the Raiders when Kansas City pitched a 31-0 shutout with just four first downs allowed in Week 7 last year.

“I’ve always had a lot of respect for Geno,” Spags said. “I’ve always had a great deal of respect for how smart he is and his rocket arm; he has a really strong arm. I put like three clips on yesterday of him from one side of the field throwing all the way [to the other], an out cut, deep to a number of different receivers. You know how talented and young they are, and they can all run that route. So we’re alerted to what kind of quarterback we’re dealing with.”

Spagnuolo then alluded to the Jets’ league-leading six players with 100-yard games this season, including running back Braelon Allen, who has stepped in since a groin injury to starter Breece Hall; Hall is expected to play on Sunday afternoon, but both backs look like threats to the coach.

“Allen has had four really good games, and it feels like they want to feature the running back no matter who’s back there,” Spagnuolo pointed out. “I think they’re a little bit different, and yet I think they both run the scheme really well.”

I think he looks Derrick Henry-ish to me sometimes,” Spags described Allen. ”He’s a big guy. So, we’ve got to be on point tackling.”

It will all start with run defense, where Kansas City ranks eighth in rushing yards allowed per game (96) and third in yards per rushing attempt (3.5). The Seahawks ran for 153 yards a couple of weeks ago, but no other opponent has hit 120 or more yards against the Chiefs on the ground this season.

item.title: Ben Roethlisberger says Steelers RB Jaylen Warren belongs in MVP conversation
item.description: The legendary quarterback knows the Steelers star back deserves much more attention.
item.content:encoded:
It’s hard to put into words just how important Jaylen Warren has been to the Steelers’ success this season. The running back’s 998 scrimmage yards through eight weeks of action is good for third in the league behind only Jahmyr Gibbs and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. There is no doubt that Warren is playing at an elite level, and people are starting to have some serious conversations about the way the back has been playing.

Former Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger recently went as far as to say that Warren deserves MVP consideration for his play so far this season on his “Footbahlin with Ben Roethlisberger” podcast.

“This guy needs to start to be talked about in some MVP stuff. Like league MVP or offensive MVP,” Roethlisberger said. “His numbers and some of the stuff he’s doing is pretty impressive. His yards after contact have to be some of the highest in the league. There’s a lot of things that don’t look good and then all of a sudden it’s like, oh, he fell forward for three.”

Warren is averaging 4.89 yards per touch so far this season, the most by any running back with at least 100 touches. Despite his incredible efficiency and performance this season, there are still 16 players with higher odds to win the NFL’s Offensive Player of the Year award on FanDuel Sportsbook.

Is Warren a value play? Possibly, but the clear reason for the lack of love for Warren comes from the fact that he only has three touchdowns this season. Despite being a workhouse and the best player on Pittsburgh’s offense, the touchdown output, coupled with the Steelers not being a flashy offense, hurts his chances significantly.

All of this to say that Roethlisberger is absolutely correct in saying Warren deserves significantly more attention than he is getting for the unbelievable season he is in the midst of having for the Steelers.

The Daily Slop – 6 November 2026

Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

Washington Post (paywall)

How Jayden Daniels turned protecting the football into his ‘superpower’

Through all of the Commanders’ struggles, the quarterback has remained one of the NFL’s most efficient passers.

Ahead of his freshman year of college in 2019, Jayden Daniels sat down with then-Arizona State coach Herm Edwards. The quarterback had been an excellent decision-maker in high school, but the former NFL coach wanted to drill home that the margin for error was about to shrink. He figured that Daniels had a future playing on Sundays and wanted to prepare him for what would come next.

“He always told me, ‘No matter what, you give yourself a chance to win the game if the possession always ends with a kick,’” Daniels told The Washington Post. “Whether that’s a punt or a field goal, you always want to end it with a kick.”

That was ingrained in Daniels throughout his five years of college football, and it hasn’t changed in the slightest through his third season with the Washington Commanders. Among the 33 NFL quarterbacks who’ve attempted at least 100 passes this season, he’s the only one who hasn’t committed a turnover.

Few quarterbacks have been better than Daniels at protecting the football since he entered the NFL in 2024. He has an interception rate of just 1.5 percent (the fourth lowest among quarterbacks who attempted at least 500 passes during that span). Overall, he’s committed just 14 turnovers (tied for the fewest).

“You just got to be locked in for six seconds each play,” Daniels said. “It kind of just goes with the flow of the game. And then, also, just having that discipline of like, ‘Okay, if it’s not there, don’t force it.’”

Sports Illustrated

Commanders Mailbag: Is Luke McCaffrey Being Overlooked? Did Dan Quinn Win Back Trust?

With Terry McLaurin out for the year, McCaffrey’s limited role on offense is harder to overlook. Plus, what the Eagles win did—and didn’t—change for Dan Quinn.

Luke McCaffrey looked good on that long kickoff return, but he barely played on offense. With Terry out for the year, is there a reason he still isn’t getting more opportunities at receiver?

Question from Nigel F. via email

That’s a great question that I’ve written about here before. From what I can tell, the staff likes McCaffrey, or he wouldn’t be on the roster, but he somehow keeps falling outside of the group that gets the main share of the offensive snaps at receiver. Against Philadelphia, McCaffrey played just three offensive snaps. Antonio Williams played 50, Treylon Burks 40, and Stefon Diggs 39. The team loaded up at receiver this offseason, giving the staff options even after McLaurin went down.

The receiver room may not be big on names outside of McLaurin and Stefon Diggs, but rookie Antonio Williams is emerging fast, and whenever Treylon Burks can stay healthy, he routinely produces. Add in the attention tight end Chig Okonkwo gets, and there’s not much left for McCaffrey, Dyami Brown, or Van Jefferson. On film, McCaffrey gets open, so offensive coordinator David Blough has to make the scheme work with the talent they have. With injuries playing a factor, McCaffrey will likely get his shot to show what he brings to the field before the end of the season.

The Athletic (paywall)

Commanders’ grand offensive transformation remains a work in progress

The Washington Commanders didn’t start over completely after their 2025 season ended with only a handful of wins. A month after the team moved on from its previous coordinators, coach Dan Quinn reintroduced David Blough, previously the assistant quarterbacks coach, as his new play caller and they laid out their basic vision of the offense.

Blough’s would be “an aggressive, balanced attack,” Quinn said, with more under-center formations and a departure from the no-huddle system Jayden Daniels had grown accustomed to over the past two years. It would require the young quarterback to get comfortable with relaying play calls — some of them lengthy — then quickly reading the defense to make any checks at the line of scrimmage.

Among the more noticeable changes: Daniels would work under center more and no longer operate almost exclusively from the shotgun formation.

“I think it opens up some different schemes in the run game, some things that I believe in,” Blough explained in February. “It opens up different play actions and keepers and getting him on the perimeter in different ways. I think there’s a level of communication that happens under center. … I think a lot of teams that you saw even playing deep into the playoffs, it was something that was a foundation of what they did.”

The goal, both Quinn and Blough said, was to create a more explosive system that would take advantage of Daniels’ accuracy and running without asking him to do everything for the offense.

Throughout the offseason, Blough, a first-time play caller, collaborated with his assistants and sought the input of his players as they built a system they said would be exclusively theirs. The foundation was an amalgamation of the offenses Blough ran during his years as a quarterback, and drawing from the offenses run by Washington’s previous play caller, Kliff Kingsbury, as well as Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell and even Louisville coach Jeff Brohm, whom Blough played for at Purdue.

The crux of the Commanders’ offense, however, would draw from Ben Johnson, Blough’s former coordinator in Detroit who has since transformed the Chicago Bears’ offense with his heavy use of play action, multiple tight end sets, outside zone run concepts and pre-snap motion.

OFF SCRIPT: Austin Ekeler wasn’t sure he’d play again. He was OK with that.

The Commanders running back opens up about nearly retiring after tearing his Achilles, AI’s upside and scary possibilities, growing up in rural Colorado and the NFL statistic he treasures most.

ASHBURN, Va. — Austin Ekeler thought he had reached the finish line of his playing career.

Not necessarily while lying on the Lambeau Field grass in pain after tearing his right Achilles. But soon after the non-contact injury in Week 2 that ended his 2025 season, any quiet time became a mental battle.

“I’m probably done,” Ekeler thought. “Probably retiring.”

The entire picture of his work and life put the injury into perspective. The running back was a workhorse for much of his seven-year stint with the Chargers. He helped the Washington Commanders reach the NFC Championship Game in season 8. Then Ekeler tore his Achilles in Year 9. He would be 31 if he returned.

2025 was also the first year he became a father. Ekeler and his wife, Melanie, welcomed a baby boy into the world that May. The guy who grew up on a farm in rural Northern Colorado was already busy “ripping projects,” from coding to creating apps to business and real estate investing. He loves football, but it’s not his life.

And yet…

“I told myself, ‘Look, let’s focus on the rehab. Don’t focus on whether I’m done or not. Don’t make that decision while I’m emotional. Continue to rehab, and then once that’s done, let’s get back in shape.”

Ekeler is a gym guy, so he would get back into shape regardless.

“Then, if I start to feel good and people are calling about me, I’ll do a workout. If they want to have me in, great. If not, let’s go rip some more code and build some more projects. That’s what it was for me.”

The calls did come. The Carolina Panthers checked in and were set to add Ekeler to their practice squad when Washington raised the stakes with a spot on the active roster.

Trey Amos Is Not Here to Save the Commanders’ Defense

After being sidelined for almost a year, the second-year cornerback made his much-anticipated return in Week 6.
If there’s one play that illustrates the value that cornerback Trey Amos brings to the Commanders defense, it’s a pass breakup from the second quarter of Sunday’s win over the Eagles.

With Philadelphia facing a third-and-2 from their own 35-yard line, Amos was matched up against Makai Lemon. The rookie receiver faked a quick slant toward the middle of the field before planting his right foot and taking off on a go route.

But before Lemon could get past him, Amos, playing in just his second game in 358 days, shoved his left arm into the wideout’s shoulder pads, forcing him to go further left and buying time as quarterback Tanner McKee launched a 25-yard bomb in the pair’s direction.

Just when it looked like the Commanders were set to give up yet another explosive pass play, Amos stretched his lanky, 6-foot-1 frame and knocked the ball away. Philadelphia punted, and the Commanders soon capitalized with more points in what would be a 27-10 win.

“That’s a difficult play, and you need length and body control to get yourself in a position to go do that,” coach Dan Quinn said Monday. “And so, the more plays, the more reps — you just know he’s gonna gain more comfort in playing.”

Amos fractured his left fibula in Week 10 last season, costing him the final eight weeks of his rookie season. Subsequent injuries over the offseason delayed his 2026 debut until Week 6. After the promise he showed as a rookie — six pass breakups and just one touchdown allowed — his return could be a major boost to a defense that’s allowing the seventh-most points (26.0) and sixth-most passing yards (243.0) per game.

What turned around Washington’s defense?

ASHBURN, Va. — Midway through the first quarter Sunday, the Washington Commanders ‘ offseason vision for its pass rush came to light. They showed seven defenders at the line of scrimmage; both inside linebackers stood at the line on either side of the center.

Then came the organized chaos and, for Washington, the fun. And a blueprint for what the Commanders (2-4-1) need to compensate for losing its top two defensive linemen, if it wants to turn its season around — starting Sunday vs. the Rams (4-4).

After all, they spent nearly $100 million in guaranteed money in the offseason to help the pass rush. It needs to help lead any resurgence and that was the case in Week 8.

“It was definitely a snapshot of what we can be,” Washington defensive coordinator Daronte Jones said. “Now it’s just about consistency.”

If they find it, it would provide a big boost — especially with linemen Daron Payne and Javon Kinlaw both out for the season.

“The better we are,” outside linebacker Dorance Armstrong said of the pass rush, “the better our defense is. Everyone knows that.”

Numerous plays showed their ability to pressure the passer. But this third-down play vs. the Eagles in Week 8 showed what can happen when they work more together, as Jones and coach Dan Quinn have wanted.

Commanders rookie Antonio Williams earning trust early from teammates

Wide receiver Antonio Williams is making the most of his opportunities in Washington, relying on preparation, confidence and relationships he’s building.

ASHBURN, Va. — With injuries impacting the Washington Commanders’ offense, rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams is stepping into a bigger role and making the most of his opportunities.

Williams has earned the confidence of his coaches and teammates, including head coach Dan Quinn, who said the rookie established trust within the organization early on.

“We have confidence in him, the quarterbacks do. That plays a big part, honestly,” Quinn said. “Like building trust among teammates, coaches — he did that very early.”

Quarterback Jayden Daniels pointed to Williams’ ability to deliver in critical moments, including a key second-down reception late in a game.

“Late in that game, that big second down, I wanna say, second-and-nine. He made that big catch down the field,” Daniels said. “Just those reps that we had at practice and that trust that we built.”

For Williams, that trust comes from preparation and consistency. He said performing at the level he expects of himself has helped him become more confident at the NFL level.

Jonathan Taylor trade rumors: NY Giants, everyone else, waiting on Colts

Hey, Colts, can we get a decision already?

“Has Jonathan Taylor been traded yet?”

Admit it, New York Giants fans. You check your favorite website (this one, I hope) multiple times a day hoping to find the answer to that question. You are checking social media constantly waiting for word. In the car, you’ve got the radio tuned to your favorite sports talk show hoping you don’t miss the news.

Well, guess what. Taylor is just like you. He wants to know what the Indianapolis Colts are doing to do, too.

‘Everybody wants clarity’

That was Taylor, the hotly sought-after running back, on Thursday.

Will the Colts decide to keep him? Will Taylor be a Giant? A Denver Bronco? A Seattle Seahawk? A Minnesota Viking? A Cincinnati Bengal?

The speculation has been running rampant for weeks, ever since Indianapolis fired GM Chris Ballard. It picked up in intensity when the Colts moved on from star guard Quenton Nelson and veteran defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.

“Everybody wants clarity,” Taylor said. “No one wants uncertainty.”

Taylor is ready for the guessing game to be over.

“The past couple weeks, it’s kind of been the same thing,” Taylor said Thursday of the rampant trade speculation about him. “But it won’t be Tuesday at that time (because) then you’ll know exactly what’s going on. You’ll know exactly what the verdict is.”

‘The New York Giants really want him’

That was Ralph Vacchiano of FOX Sports writing about the Giants’ desire to complete a deal for the 27-year-old Taylor.

Cowboys at Colts: Offensive, defensive impact players in Week 9

Two Cowboys who should have a big impact on Sunday

Whether it’s due to talent or circumstances, certain players impact the game more than others week in and week out. The Dallas Cowboys have several such players who can help turn the tide at any moment in any given game. To hopefully get their season back on track and start stacking some wins together, they need these players to step up now more than ever.

In the Week 9 matchup with the Indianapolis Colts we believe the Cowboys have a player on each side of the ball who will impact the game in a big way in this week, and we discuss why these two individuals should help sway the game in the Cowboys favor.

Offense – RB Javonte Williams

The offensive game plan and play-calling for Brian Schottenheimer should be an easy one this week, run the ball early and often. The Indianapolis Colts currently ranked 27th in the league in run defense, allowing 131.8 rushing yards per game.

What is Rams’ plan for Ty Simpson?

Through eight weeks, Stetson Bennett is still Matthew Stafford’s backup. What is the plan for Ty Simpson?

The Los Angeles Rams had a plan to futureproof the quarterback position. They hid their intentions well during the spring before shocking the NFL by selecting Ty Simpson with the thirteenth overall pick.

But a plan—at least a good one—doesn’t stop at drafting a player.

We knew Simpson was a green prospect entering the draft. He looked as ready as you possibly could during the preseason. For someone who the consensus said needed time to develop, Simpson looked poised under pressure and kept the ball out of harm’s way during the exhibition games.

Through eight weeks Simpson has been a healthy scratch on game days. He still dressed as the emergency third quarterback behind Matthew Stafford and Stetson Bennett, although he cannot step onto the field unless the two signal callers ahead of him are unavailable because of injury.

item.title: Giants’ offense vs. Eagles’ defense: The Vic Fangio factor
item.description: Can the Giants offense remain explosive against the Philadelphia Eagles?
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants emerge as winners from their Week 8 BYE.

They’re (relatively) rested and still riding the emotional wave of a stunning overtime win in Week 7. They return to action this week as 3.5-point favorites (per FanDuel) on the road against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Eagles have been in a tailspin over the last several weeks, losing the last six games. They’ve lost each of the last three games by at least 11 points, including a deflating 27-10 loss to the Washington Commanders last week.

The Giants are looking to build on the momentum of their upset win over the Houston Texans, while the Eagles are just hoping to stop the skid.

What can J.J. McCarthy and the Giants’ offense expect from the Eagles’ defense?

Stats that matter

Can J.J. McCarthy do it again?

The last six (counting overtime) quarters of Giants’ football have turned former 10th overall pick J.J. McCarthy into a national story. Most had written McCarthy off after his rookie year was upended by injury, his sophomore year was a disappointment, and he fell to QB3 in his third year.

Now? McCarthy has catapulted himself back into the “QB1” conversation with an electric 11 minutes against the New Orleans Saints and a game full of explosive plays against the Houston Texans. This of course, begs the question: Can he do it again?

The Eagles now have about a game and a half worth of tape on the McCarthy-led Giants. That isn’t much to go on, but it may be enough to form a more effective gameplan.

The good news is that McCarthy also has two more weeks in the Giants’ offense and more tme practicing with the Giants’ starters. Not to mention, McCarthy will get to enjoy the presence of a (hopefully) healthier Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor. It seems likely that Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio will look to contain the explosive passing plays that defined his performance against the Texans. McCarthy excelled at throwing deep against Houston, delivering some legitimate “WOW” throws. He’ll need to capitalize on the opportunities to do so against the Eagles, but can’t count on them being regular occurrences. Instead, the Giants’ intermediate passing game will need to be more consistent on a down-to-down basis while they work to create opportunities for explosive plays.

If there was a blemish on McCarthy’s game against the Texans, it’s that his passing success rate* was 25th out of 25 qualifying quarterbacks.

*Success rate is defined as the rate at which a play that gains a percentage of the yards needed to convert a first down. A “successful” first down picks up 40 percent of the yards to convert, a successful second down picks up 60 percent of the yards to convert, and a successful third down picks up 100 percent of the yards to convert.

Explosive plays are great and go a long way toward making it more likely that a team scores on a given drive. However, a team can’t rely on explosive plays to consistently move the ball down the field. While the Giants did an excellent job of scheming 1-on-1 opportunities and good receiving windows downfield for McCarthy, it’s not something they can live on. McCarthy will need to be more consistent in hitting underneath passes to keep the offense moving and on schedule. That will be particularly true if the Giants’ run game struggles with both Cam Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy injured.

Will the run game show up?

The Giants finally got their run game going against the Texans. While the Texans’ defense isn’t what it was in 2025, they still filed one of the NFL’s best run defenses, which makes the Giants’ 180-yard, 3-touchdown performance all the more impressive.

The Eagles’ run defense has decidedly mediocre this year. And their high Run Stop Win Rate but average YPC and high rushing EPA allowed (+11.45, 28th in the NFL) suggest that they’re prone to giving up explosive plays on the ground. That would be good news for the Giants in light of their performance against the Texans, but there are suddenly doubts about the Giants’ backfield.

Tyrone Tracy landed on injured reserve with a hamstring injury suffered early in the game, while Cam Skattebo is currently not practicing with a hamstring injury of his own. Skattebo’s injury was suffered at the end of his final carry of the game, the 42-yard run which set up Devin Singletary’s 30-yard touchdown run to win the game. Skattebo ended that run early when he felt his hamstring tighten, and while he didn’t seem overly concerned after the game, he has yet to practice.

That leaves Singletary and the newly-added Greg Desrosiers as the Giants’ healthy backfield, with practice squad backs Phil Mafah and Eric Gray as possible additions.

The Giants offensive line will need to play well. While the Eagles’ defense has struggled this year, the trio of Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and Moro Ojomo remains dangerous.

The Giants will also need to depend on McCarthy’s play to help unlock their running game. Not only will more consistent passing success help take the pressure off the run game, but the threat of McCarthy’s legs will help unlock the running game. The Giants used a slow mesh to simulate a read-option play on Tyrone Tracy’s touchdown, freezing a key Texans’ defender. The Giants could make (judicious) use of the read-option with McCarthy in this game — as they did with Jaxson Dart in Week 1 against Fangio acolyte Christian Parker — to help supplement their rushing attack.

The Giants could also make use of Darnell Mooney as a pseudo-running back with sweeps and screen plays. Mooney has been disappointing as a receiver, but his athleticism and explosiveness have been apparent when he gets the ball in his hands. Doing so on schemed touches could be a way the Giants look to augment their rushing attack and adding an explosive element on the ground.

Facing Fangio

The Giants have spent most of the 2026 season facing defenses we’ve called “Fangio Adjacent”. That is, defenses designed and called by coaches who have either been inspired by Vic Fangio, or his acolytes.

We’ve already been over the iterations enough to know the general shape of the “Fangio” defense.

It’s based around a 4-2-5 nickel formation under a quarters coverage. He makes heavy use of pattern matching principles to add man coverage to his zone schemes, as well as using post-snap rotations to create ambiguity and doubt in quarterbacks’ reads. While his defenses frequently start out in a Cover-4 look, they often rotate to Cover 3, adding a defender to the box, or a hybrid coverage like Cover-6 or Cover-8* to give them a numbers advantage to the passing strength.

*I go into more detail on Cover-6 and Cover-8 in our Week 1 preview of the Cowboys’ defense.

Fangio doesn’t blitz all that often, just 22.5% of the time (26th in the NFL), instead trusting his defensive front to get home.

While the details may shift with different coordinators and defensive rosters, the basic shape of the “Fangio” defense remains consistent and has become one of the most popular philosophies in the NFL. However, the biggest advantage that Fangio himself has always been that it’s his. More than any other coach, Fangio not only knows how is defense is able to attack offenses, but is also intimately aware of it’s weaknesses and how offenses go about attacking his scheme.

We saw that first-hand last year when Fangio deviated from his scheme on Thursday Night Football. That game he opted to blitz Dart heavily in his second start. Fangio has typically eschewed the blitz, instead trusting his defensive front to get pressure while playing coverage behind them. While the decision to blitz a rookie is typically correct, it proved disastrous against Dart. The weaknesses were easily exploited by the athletic young quarterback, and it stressed the defense in ways that it wasn’t designed to sustain.

Two weeks later, Fangio went back to his roots and played his usual coverages and didn’t blitz Dart. This time, the rookie struggled to identify the post-snap rotations and had one of his worst performances of a rookie year that was largely otherwise promising.

McCarthy was excellent when the Houston Texans employed MOFC (middle of field closed) looks. Whether it was Cover-1 (man) or Cover-3 (zone), single-high safety looks created defined passing lanes for McCarthy and he took advantage. While it’s notable that the Giants’ rushing offense finally got going against the Texans, their explosive passing attack helped carry the day when Houston’s defense got them off schedule.

We should expect Fangio and the Eagles to be well aware of this and try to stick to their usual two-high shells against McCarthy.

The good news for the Giants is that the Eagles’ pressure rates have been simply bad this year, as they’ve bled talent from their Super Bowl roster of two years ago. They might be forced to try and blitz McCarthy if he’s too comfortable in the pocket, which could create weaknesses which the Giants could exploit.

We should also expect the Giants to make a concerted effort to run the ball and attack the second level of the field with Isaiah Likely, Malachi Fields, and their running backs. Doing so effectively could also help to force the Eagles out of their two-deep shells and into more vulnerable looks.

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 9 Start/Sit Advice: What to do with Ashton Jeanty, Jaylen Waddle, more players
item.description: Scott Pianowski plays traffic cop, helping you with some of those tough fantasy football lineup calls for Week 9.
item.content:encoded:
Start-sit decisions can be vexing for even the best of fantasy football managers. If you need help setting your fantasy football lineups, Scott Pianowski offers some assistance with his Week 9 traffic report.

Green Light ✅

RB Chase Brown vs. Falcons (Spain): The Bengals don't have a major challenger to Brown in the backfield, and the Atlanta defense has been much better against the pass in 2026. Brown probably has 15-plus touches off the plane this week, and given the messiness in the RB streets, that keeps him afloat as a lower-end RB2.

QB Kirk Cousins at 49ers: The Raiders have struggled to run the ball all year — even the switch to Mike Washington Jr. was an efficiency bust last week. Look for Cousins to throw 40 or more times against the Niners in this spot, given expected game flow and the shape of the San Francisco defense (weaker against the pass). I'm not afraid to go back to WR Tre Tucker, either.

QB Malik Willis vs. Lions: He's started to improve over the last three weeks (QB14, QB4, QB15), adding some passing production to go with his weekly rushing floor. And the Detroit defense is a lovely draw, the leakiest secondary to attack in the league. Also keep the light on for TE Greg Dulcich, as the Lions are especially vulnerable down the seam.

WR Adonai Mitchell at Chiefs: The Kansas City defense has been a funnel this year, stingy against the run but gettable versus the pass. Mitchell's music can keep playing here, especially if Garrett Wilson (concussion) isn't ready to return. The Jets aren't going anywhere at 2-6, but they've had a legitimate offense all year.

WR DeMario Douglas vs. Packers: He's scored four times in four weeks and has 17 catches on his last 20 targets, building rapport with Drake Maye. The Patriots might be without both A.J. Brown and Hunter Henry in this spot, pushing Douglas into a possible opportunity spike.

Yellow Light 😕

QB Brock Purdy vs. Raiders: All the algorithms are suggesting I should elevate Purdy to my starting lineup, but with Mike Evans and Deebo Samuel Sr. likely out, I've got cold feet. Teammates matter, and the 49ers have had a ridiculous run of WR injuries. Look for San Francisco to aggressively work the phones for a trade over the next few days.

RB Tyler Allgeier at Seahawks: He's all the Cardinals have in the backfield, with Jeremiyah Love (ankle) out and Bam Knight still in concussion protocol. Perhaps Allgeier can do something similar to what D'Andre Swift managed in Seattle last week, scoring points on volume and goal-line opportunity even if the efficiency doesn't pop. With solid backs like Tony Pollard and Jaylen Warren on bye this week, many managers need to be open-minded on Allgeier.

RB Alvin Kamara vs Browns: With Travis Etienne Jr. not ready to return, the PPR scam could be open for Kamara again. He caught seven passes the last time we saw the Saints, and he'll likely collect 5-7 rushing attempts too, even if those seldom turn into much. The bar for RB2/RB3 relevance has never been so low.

WR Ryan Flournoy at Colts: It's not easy to punch a ticket on a team's No. 3 wideout, but Flournoy has found double-digit points in three of his past four starts, basically replacing Jake Ferguson as the third pitch in this passing game. If George Pickens is limited or unavailable on game day, Flournoy would have a puncher's chance at 8-10 targets. Flournoy offers deep-flex value in the moment and could be a key player later in the season if injuries hit elsewhere.

RB Blake Corum at Commanders: He's had double-digit touches in three straight games and he's found the end zone in three of four weeks. The Rams' backfield is almost a 50-50 show at the moment, and Los Angeles should control game flow against the overmatched Commanders. Corum has worked his way into the RB2 conversation.

Red Light 🚨

WR Jaylen Waddle at Panthers: The touchdown was nice last week, but Waddle hasn't topped 50 yards in his last six starts. The Denver passing game has looked broken all year, and even with Carolina dealing with cluster injuries in the secondary, I can't invest in any Denver wideout.

WR Michael Wilson at Seahawks: He'll aim top play through two broken ribs, but the matchup couldn't be worse, the nasty Seahawks in a get-right spot. Gardner Minshew was a miracle worker late last week, but that's the type of story that often corrects the following week.

WR Chris Godwin Jr. at Bears: He's starting to look like a compromised player in his 10th season, and somehow the Buccaneers haven't thrown for 200 yards in a single game this year. Emeka Egbuka (foot) is trending for a return this week, which is further bad news for Godwin. It might be time to cut the name-brand veteran.

RB Ashton Jeanty at 49ers: It's not clear if his role change last week was more a soft benching or something sustainable moving forward. But we can't ignore that Mike Washington Jr. has been a more efficient runner this year, and the Niners might force the Raiders to junk the running game anyway. Jeanty is best left on benches while the Raiders give us a clearer reveal on their backfield plans.

item.title: Patriots will have their hands full against Packers’ explosive passing game
item.description: Eliminating big plays top the Patriots’ list of defensive priorities against the Packers.
item.content:encoded:
The Green Bay Packers offense has had its ups and downs this season, as evidenced by the fact it is ranked 20th in points (21.4) and 18th in yards per game (331.6) as well as 17th in expected points added per play (0.010). One area that has consistently yielded positive results so far, however, has been its deep game.

No team in the NFL has had more explosive plays in the passing game than the Packers, who have had 33 plays of 20-plus yards so far this season. Quarterback Jordan Love, meanwhile, is tied for the league lead with 17 completions of 20-plus air yards, and tied for third in average depth of target (9.8).

The New England Patriots therefore know what’s in store this Sunday.

“This team lives off of taking shots,” said safety Kevin Byard. “They’re an explosive-play team, a vertical-passing team. So, this will be a huge challenge for us as a defense. Obviously trying to be sticky in coverage, but also when we are playing zone, making sure we’re getting back in our zones, making sure we’re actually forcing those checkdowns. And sometimes I think in this game we’re going to have to accept the four- or five-yard checkdowns and not allowing the ball to get thrown over our head.”

Through eight games this year, the Patriots defense has been uneven stopping the big passing play. In total, the unit has surrendered 25 of them — 10th-worst in the league.

Patriots fans, join the game-day huddle!

Follow every snap and discuss every decision with fellow fans on the SB Nation app.

  • Connect through our live game chat
  • Browse with fewer ads
  • Seamlessly move between communities
  • Enjoy faster commenting and posting

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Staying on the average so far could yield catastrophic results against a team like the Packers, that has specialized in taking the top off of defenses. Green Bay has been able to do so in large part due to its top wide receiver duo, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden.

Watson is leading the team with 708 receiving yards and six touchdowns on 42 catches, an average of 16.9 yards per reception. Golden has caught 43 passes for 619 yards, four scores, and 14.4 yards per catch. Together, they have been responsible for 54 of Green Bay’s 97 passing first downs this year.

“These receivers are explosive, especially Watson and Golden. That’s a nasty duo there about taking the top off,” said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr.

“Christian Watson may be the fastest receiver in the league; he’s always a big play threat anytime he touches the ball,” added Byard. “But also Matthew Golden — he is a second-year player — has a lot of juice. He’s building a really good rapport. I know he’s dropped some passes and stuff like that, but he’s getting open. He’s creating separation.”

Drops have indeed been a problem for the Packers, with Golden leading the league with nine of them this year. In total, Green Bay’s pass catchers have let 23 passes go through their hands. What this goes to show, however, is that the team’s potential for big plays has been even greater than the eventual statistics shows.

A lot of that is not just due to the receiving talent, but the quarterback himself.

“I think he’s one of the most underrated quarterbacks in this league,” said Byard about Jordan Love. “He doesn’t get put into the top-10 lists sometimes, but he’s very efficient. He’s leading the league in passing yards right now. He’s having a career year. A lot of it is because of those deep ball shots.”

“He hunts explosives,” said Kuhr. “They can meticulously drive down the field and sometimes that’s what it’s got to be, but we have to try to limit those 20-plus-yard plays, and they are really good at it. He’s really good at it. He throws a great deep ball. … We have to do our best to try to defend that in more than just one way. We can’t just be, ‘Hey, we’re going to pressure him and make it get off quick, and we’re not covering as long.‘ And it’s also, ‘Hey, we can’t just sit back forever.‘ We have to be able to mix it up a little bit.”

The Patriots’ defensive success on Sunday might depend on their ability to do just that.

item.title: Fantasy Football Week 9 Fades & Busts: Bad times to continue for Panthers
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Matt Okada highlights the players we need to temper expectations for in Week 9.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to the ninth of 17 weekly articles spotlighting the fantasy fades of the week! I am your host, Matt Okada, and I'll be bringing you half a dozen potential busts each and every Friday, from now until fantasy football championships.

As a note, just because a player earns a "fade" or "bust" designation doesn't automatically mean they should be benched — it depends on the rest of your roster or the options on your waiver wire. But you can expect them to fall short of expectations (when I get them right). I include a "What to Do" section for every player to help with that.

Without further ado, here is my list for Week 9 of the 2026 season.

Bryce Young, QB, Panthers vs. Broncos

Over the first two weeks of the season, Bryce Young was brilliant, throwing for three touchdowns and hitting 24+ fantasy points in both games. Then, he suffered a minor knee injury in Week 3, which he has played through with a brace, limiting his mobility in the pocket. He hasn't thrown three touchdowns in any of Carolina's six contests since, clocking in at just seven TDs and four interceptions over that span.

In the meantime, the Panthers' offensive line has been ravaged by injuries and, in combination, these factors have led to a severe drop-off in fantasy production for Young. He's been pressured on 50% of his dropbacks over the last two weeks and has logged a 35.4 passer rating and 20% success rate against that pressure. Largely as a result, he's averaged just 9.39 fantasy points per game in those two outings.

Now, he draws a matchup with a Broncos defense sporting the league's fourth-highest pressure rate (40.3%) and second-highest quick pressure rate (21.7%), per Next Gen Stats, both of which have increased in recent weeks. Young is likely to be in trouble early and often in this game and is staring down the barrel of another fantasy dud.

What to do ❓ Young is well outside QB1 range and is honestly closer to the back of QB2 range this week. I'd much prefer a streamer like Tyler Shough, Malik Willis, Kirk Cousins or even Michael Penix Jr.

Ollie Gordon II, RB, Dolphins vs. Lions

Ollie Gordon II has been shockingly good for fantasy since taking over for De'Von Achane several weeks ago. Most of the fantasy community couldn't even decide whether he'd get the starting job, and he's proceeded to average 18.8 touches per game since the Week 3 takeover and score 13+ fantasy points in four of those five contests. However, I'm pumping the brakes for Week 9.

Coming off his first dud — 6.9 points against the tough Patriots run defense — Gordon has an even tougher matchup in the Lions. Detroit is a massive pass-funnel opponent, meaning that it encourages offenses to throw — allowing a league-high 298.7 yards per game on a league-high 41 attempts per game — rather than run (where it's bottom-10 in YPG and attempts per game allowed). As a result, it's allowing the fourth-fewest fantasy points per game to running backs. And unfortunately, Gordon has essentially zero role in the Miami passing attack. If he's lucky enough to see a goal-line carry or two, Gordon could score a touchdown and eke out a decent fantasy day, but it feels far more likely that he has another medium-volume, low-efficiency day and ends up in single-digit fantasy points once again.

What to do ❓ Gordon isn't an absolute must-sit, especially given the shallow nature of the position. But he's a low-end RB2 at best and I'd definitely lower expectations and avoid him in DFS.

Jordan Mason, RB, Vikings vs. Bills

Speaking of the Lions' run defense, they turned Jordan Mason into an absolute dud last week, with just 20 rushing yards on eight carries for 2.0 fantasy points. That brings his total since returning from injury in Week 7 to 88 yards on 23 carries (3.8 per carry) with zero catches and zero touchdowns. Fantasy managers who waited on his return are justifiably frustrated but might see a glimmer of hope in the "green" Bills matchup here in Week 9.

Not so fast.

Buffalo has been a good matchup for running backs because its allowed the third-most receiving fantasy points per game, at 11.0, behind only the Dolphins and 49ers. In rushing fantasy points, its much closer to the middle of the pack, and Mason is only guaranteed to see a portion of that production with Aaron Jones Sr. still involved. The Vikings offense has been extremely lackluster all season and they're an underdog against the Bills in what figures to be a relatively low-scoring affair. None of this bodes well for the run-only half of Minnesota's RBBC, so Mason is better suited on the bench until a better opportunity arises ... if ever.

What to do ❓ Mason is well outside RB2 range and I wouldn't even consider him a promising FLEX. You're better off starting committee-backs like Zach Charbonnet or Blake Corum, as they should have better chances at scoring.

Jalen Coker, WR, Panthers vs. Broncos

Remember everything I said about Bryce Young, the Panthers' O-line and the mess that pressure has created for this passing attack lately? All of that trickles down in a very discouraging way for early breakout candidate, Jalen Coker. He has just three catches on 10 targets all season when Young is pressured and just three catches for 45 yards during this particularly troubling downturn the past two weeks. He had a brilliant game against the Eagles three weeks ago, but Philly is currently the best matchup for wide receivers, so we have to take that 97-yard game with a grain of salt. And it makes sense that pressure and Coker don't get along: he's averaged 11.2 air yards per target and 20.5% of his targets have come on deep passes this season (nearly twice as high as the rate for Tetairoa McMillan).

Meanwhile, Denver has allowed the fifth-fewest fantasy points to wide receivers and the fourth-fewest yards per target on downfield throws (10+ air yards). Just as Young is a fade, Coker is a complementary fade for all the same reasons. I like his upside down the stretch if Young and the O-line can get healthy, but he's a very risky play in the meantime.

What to do ❓ Coker is outside WR2 range and while he's a playable FLEX in a pinch, I'd rather go with a lesser name in a better situation, like Keenan Allen or Stefon Diggs.

Jaylen Waddle, WR, Broncos at Panthers

It seems like there's a bit of growing optimism about Jaylen Waddle in the fantasy community ... but I'm not entirely sure why. Sure, he caught a touchdown in Week 8 against the Chiefs ... just his second of the year, by the way. He also finished that game with three catches for 39 yards, marking his sixth-straight game with fewer than six catches and fewer than 50 receiving yards. His only truly impressive outing all season came back in Week 2 against the Jaguars — who have proven to be a major pass-funnel defense — when he saw eight catches for 138 yards on 10 targets. But Waddle had 138 receiving yards in his other six games combined entering Week 8 and is averaging just 39.4 per game on the season, even when including that aberration of an outing against Jacksonville.

He's averaging the fourth-fewest yards per target (6.2) among all wideouts with 50+ targets and doesn't have a game over 14 fantasy points in the last six weeks. All told, his floor and ceiling are concerningly low and I see little reason for optimism against the Panthers — even with injuries to their starting cornerbacks — given how spotty and inefficient Waddle's usage has been.

What to do ❓ Waddle falls a couple spots behind Coker in my rankings, so we can apply the same logic for him in Week 9 — WR3 at best, iffy FLEX play, would rather go with Allen or Diggs.

Dalton Kincaid, TE, Bills at Vikings

This pains me, as I am a huge Dalton Kincaid fan, and there are a lot of reasons to believe in him rest-of-season — like his position-leading 2.7 yards per route run and his robust-for-a-tight-end air yards share (19.7%). But the Minnesota Vikings are terrifying. They've allowed a league-low 5.5 fantasy points per game to tight ends and have held every single TE they've faced to single-digit fantasy points. Tucker Kraft set the current high-water mark at just 8.0 points, while Sam LaPorta (5.0), Juwan Johnson (3.6), Colston Loveland (0.8) and others have been complete duds in this matchup.

On average, they've surrendered just 3.1 catches for 39.0 yards per game to the position, and have yet to allow a touchdown to a tight end all season. Sitting Kincaid won't be easy, especially given the shallow nature of the position, but it might be necessary given the heavily reduced ceiling against Minnesota.

What to do ❓ Try to find a streamer in redraft if you can, a la T.J. Hockenson, Kyle Pitts Sr., or even Brenton Strange, rather than playing Kincaid against this defense. And stay away in DFS.
