item.title: Seahawks All-22 review: The good and bad from an ugly loss to the Bears
item.description: Seattle's loss to Chicago raises more questions about the offense and defense heading into a crucial stretch.
item.content:encoded:
Losing to the Chicago Bears isn’t exactly a shocking outcome. Ben Johnson has built a competitive team, and Chicago has shown it can hang with anyone. But the way the Seattle Seahawks lost is what should frustrate Seattle fans.

The offense struggled to sustain drives, the defense failed to make enough plays, and several issues that have followed this team throughout the season resurfaced at the worst possible time. Seattle had opportunities to make this a competitive game, but too many mistakes on both sides of the ball made that difficult.

The loss also carries significant weight in the standings. The Seahawks are now further behind the 49ers and have dropped an important head-to-head matchup against a team that could be competing with them for a Wild Card spot down the stretch. These are the kinds of games Seattle needed to win.

The Bad

Third-down struggles come back to haunt the Seahawks

Seattle’s third-down problems returned in a big way against Chicago. The Seahawks converted just 1 of 11 attempts, a dismal 9.1% conversion rate.

That’s particularly frustrating considering how well the offense had handled some difficult third-down situations against the Chiefs. Seattle had been finding ways to convert third-and-long situations at an impressive rate, but there’s a difference between being good at converting those situations and constantly putting yourself in them.

Converting third-and-long is a valuable skill, but it shouldn’t be mistaken for a sustainable offensive strategy. When an offense consistently finds itself facing long third downs, it usually means something has already gone wrong on first and second down. Whether it’s ineffective runs, poor play sequencing, or a lack of answers against the defensive front, the offense is making life harder for itself.

Eventually, a good defense is going to make you pay for that.

Chicago did exactly that. The Bears consistently put Seattle in difficult situations, and the Seahawks had no answers when it mattered.

Brian Fleury and Sam Darnold share the blame

There’s been plenty of debate among Seahawks fans about who’s more responsible for the offensive struggles. Is it Brian Fleury and his play-calling, or is it Sam Darnold and his decision-making?

The answer is pretty simple: both are to blame.

Fleury has struggled to put together a consistent offensive plan. The route concepts don’t always complement each other, the play sequencing can feel disconnected, and there are too many situations in which the offense appears to have no answer for what the defense is doing.

One example is how defenses have been sending blitzes on early downs, anticipating an under-center play-action pass. Fleury hasn’t found a way to counter those looks, repeatedly leaving Darnold under pressure.

It’s not just about individual play calls. Good offensive design should create opportunities from one play to the next, manipulate defensive reactions, and give the quarterback answers against different coverages. Too often, Seattle’s offense looks like a collection of unrelated plays rather than a cohesive system. In other words, even some creative play designs struggle to work because they aren’t connected to a larger plan.

The red zone offered another example. In this play, Darnold finishes the play without a dropback, and the routes essentially just run toward the defenders. There’s no real attempt to create space or take advantage of the double coverage on JSN. It’s discouraging to watch.

Having him call two running plays with ten minutes left in the fourth quarter, while trailing by more than one possession, was one of the strangest decisions I’ve seen in a long time. Even if it looks like Darnold changed the play the second time around, the decision itself was bizarre.

Darnold’s performance is concerning, too.

He held onto the ball too long on several occasions, missed throws he should have made, and made questionable decisions throughout the game. There were also instances in which he abandoned progressions that appeared to offer better options.

His pre-snap recognition was particularly concerning on the play that resulted in his rib injury. On the second snap of the game, Kyler Gordon lined up in an obvious blitz position. Yet Darnold didn’t appear to make any meaningful adjustment to the protection or prepare for the pressure coming from that side.

Gordon wasn’t exactly hiding his intentions. The alignment itself should have been enough to trigger an adjustment, whether that meant changing the protection or preparing to get the ball out quickly. Instead, Darnold appeared caught off guard by a pressure that should have been anticipated.

Darnold hesitates too much and abandons his reads. It’s not necessarily that he’s missing throws to completely uncovered receivers; he’s failing to hit windows that an NFL quarterback should be able to recognize and attack. Here, at the end of his dropback, he has JSN, who has confused the defensive back. With better anticipation and timing, the ball should already be on its way. On several occasions, Darnold failed to anticipate his receivers’ routes.

Here, he tries to read JSN’s release, but Kyler Gordon does a good job covering him. Darnold moves to his next read and finds Horton. However, he hesitates for a moment and puts the receiver directly in harm’s way, throwing toward the safety. It’s an exact example of what a hospital ball looks like.

Here’s a rare good play call from Fleury. Horton’s route creates separation with the cut in JSN’s route. Darnold sees it, but once again hesitates, doesn’t throw the ball, and decides to run. I’m not saying this is an easy throw, but it’s an NFL throw.

Darnold was intercepted for the ninth time, but that’s not the play I want to focus on. Instead, there’s an interception that was wiped out by a penalty. Darnold recognizes that JSN has drawn the safety’s double coverage and, once again, just as he did on his second interception against the Broncos, puts the ball where it shouldn’t go. The throw to Kupp should have been placed toward the back of the end zone, away from the defender and out of harm’s way. Instead, it goes right into the defender’s hands.

The defense wasn’t the reason Seattle lost, but it certainly didn’t help

The Bears finished with 34 points, and Caleb Williams became the first quarterback to in awhile against this Seattle defense to surpass 200 passing yards. Chicago found success through the air and on the ground, while also creating problems for the Seahawks in the red zone.

The Seahawks defense had been excellent against Kenneth Walker in its previous outing, particularly when it came to tackling. Against Chicago, that discipline disappeared.

Missed tackles repeatedly turned what should have been negative plays into significant gains. There were also opportunities to bring down the quarterback or finish plays behind the line of scrimmage that Seattle couldn’t capitalize on.

The edges remain a problem

Seattle continues to be relatively solid against the run between the tackles, but the edges have become a concerning weakness.

The defensive ends haven’t consistently generated pressure, and their run fits have also created opportunities for opposing offenses.

Take DeMarcus Lawrence, for example. At times, he attacks an interior gap that is already occupied by Ernest Jones, leaving the outside vulnerable and forcing someone like Julian Love or a cornerback to make the replacement. That alignment issue led to two touchdowns in this game alone.

Derrick Hall has also had situations in which he crashes inside and leaves the edge open for Caleb Williams to escape.

These are the kinds of mistakes that can turn an otherwise well-defended play into a significant gain. The defensive front needs to maintain its assignments, especially when facing a quarterback capable of creating plays outside the pocket.

The pass rush as a whole is another concern. Mike Macdonald’s defensive scheme is designed to create pressure through different combinations and often relies heavily on interior disruption. That means the edge defenders won’t always be the ones finishing plays with sacks. Sometimes their job is to occupy space, control the pocket, and allow other defenders to get home.

But there’s a difference between not recording sacks and failing to generate pressure altogether.

Opponents continue to attack the linebackers’ second-level coverage responsibilities

This has become a recurring issue for Seattle, and Chicago found ways to exploit it throughout the game.

The Bears repeatedly attacked the space behind the linebackers, particularly by putting Ernest Jones in difficult coverage situations. Jones has a lot of responsibilities in this defense, and opposing offenses are finding ways to make him choose between multiple threats.

The trick play here is designed to hold Jones and move him out of position, opening a window behind him. Spoon’s coverage doesn’t come off perfectly, and that creates the space needed for the pass to work.

The Bears executed this concept repeatedly, and Seattle struggled to find an answer. There were at least four instances in which Dig routes found space behind the second level of the defense.

Things get difficult when your best players aren’t playing well

There’s an old saying: when your best players have a bad night, it’s going to be a long night.

That’s exactly what happened to Seattle’s defense.

Nick Emmanwori read the route and initially took a good angle, but then struggled to adjust. What could have been an interception turned into a touchdown. He was also beaten several times throughout the night, including in man coverage against Loveland.

Leonard Williams also had a chance to make a tackle behind the line of scrimmage, potentially turning the play into a sack or a significant loss of yardage. Instead, he couldn’t finish the play, allowing the offense to gain ground.

Julian Love was late on a few plays, got lost in coverage, and dropped an interception. It wasn’t an easy catch, but it’s one he would normally come down with.

These are players Seattle expects to make a difference. They’re among the most important pieces of the defense, and the team needs them to deliver when opportunities arise.

Of course, nobody expects perfection. But when your best defenders fail to capitalize on the opportunities that could change the game, it becomes increasingly difficult to overcome the mistakes elsewhere.

The Good

Quenton Nelson makes a promising Seahawks debut

There weren’t many positives to take away from this game, but Quenton Nelson’s debut was certainly one of them.

The veteran guard had a strong performance in his first outing with Seattle, showing exactly why his addition could be so important to the offensive line.

That technique is absolutely outstanding against Grady Jarrett. This could have resulted in a huge gain if Price hadn’t hesitated.

Unfortunately, Nelson isn’t going to fix the offensive line’s problems by himself. The Bears show simulated pressure here. Nelson and Josh Jones are on one side, where there’s only one defender. Nelson looks to see what’s happening on the other side, and it’s a mess. The Bears’ linebackers run a stunt, and George Holani — who struggled in pass protection throughout the game — and Sundell fail to communicate and execute their assignments. They end up leaving a defender free to get to the quarterback. Nelson manages to slow the pressure down just enough to give Darnold a chance to make the throw.

Maybe Nelson was thinking, “Do I have to do everything myself?” On this snap, he takes down Jarrett with a double-team block and then works his way to the second level, opening up space for the running back alongside an excellent block from Jones.

Nelson played around 60 snaps and allowed just one pressure. He also had one false start and one poor run-blocking rep. Overall, it was a very encouraging debut.

Seattle should have run the ball behind him more often.

Josh Jones could make the offensive line situation interesting

Josh Jones was another pleasant surprise.

Despite a couple of mistakes, including the pressure that resulted in Seattle’s blocked field goal and two pressures allowed on the final drive, Jones had a very solid performance overall.

His hand usage stood out, as did his strength and ability to maintain his blocks. He looked technically sound for most of the game and showed that he can be a reliable option when given the opportunity.

Good work in pass protection, along with his ability to get downfield and take good angles in the running game, particularly at the second level.

His technique wasn’t just on display in a supporting role. He had an incredible snap-and-trap block against none other than Jeffery Simmons, who basically destroyed Seattle’s offensive line for most of the game.

It’s only one game, but Jones could make a case for the starting right tackle job once Cross returns, especially with Lucas playing so far below the level we’ve come to expect from him.

Final Thoughts

As mentioned earlier, the loss itself isn’t surprising. The way it happened is another story. Seattle is now essentially in must-win territory. In theory, the games against the Cardinals and Raiders, along with the bye week, give the Seahawks an opportunity to make adjustments before the final stretch of the season.

The most important thing is making sure these mistakes don’t keep happening. This team has talented coaches and players who are capable of turning things around, but every week and every loss makes the road ahead more difficult.

Go Hawks!

item.title: Our Defense vs. Their Offense: Cleveland Browns
item.description: Saints defense has a chance to show they are turning things around against a weak Browns offense
item.content:encoded:
As the New Orleans Saints’ offense has been the primary focus coming out of the bye week, the defense should not be ignored. Defensively, the Saints have had some obvious struggles, and this matchup against the Browns is a battle of weak against weak.

The Browns enter this game with questions surrounding starting quarterback Deshaun Watson, as he entered concussion protocol earlier this week. That means, as of this moment, Shedeur Sanders is slated to make his first start of the 2026 campaign.

The loss of Watson will be a significant challenge for the Browns to overcome, but they weren’t exactly setting the world on fire offensively with him.

The Browns enter this week averaging 301 yards per game in total offense, which ranks 24th in the league. They rush for only 97 yards per game and throw for 204, ranking 24th and 22nd, respectively. They are also near the bottom of the league in scoring, averaging just 17 points per game, and rank dead last in pass protection, having allowed a league-worst 33 sacks in eight games.

This is an offense that a defense should be able to take advantage of.

The problem is that the Saints have a defense that an offense can take advantage of.

This game feels like the Vikings game, when Minnesota’s offense wasn’t particularly good, but the Saints’ defense wasn’t either. The Vikings went on to have a very impressive day in the Dome.

The Browns feature several players the Saints will have to keep their eyes on.

Running back Quinshon Judkins is the primary rushing threat. So far this season, he is averaging only 3.4 yards per carry, but he has game-breaking talent. Matching up against a weak run defense like the Saints’ could be just what the young back needs to ignite a resurgence.

Given the uncertainty surrounding Watson’s health, running the ball will likely be the focal point of the Browns’ offense.

The Saints will have to stop Judkins.

When the Browns look to pass, they will utilize a variety of weapons. Harold Fannin Jr. is a tight end, but he is also the team’s leading receiver. The Saints cannot allow Fannin to have a Brock Bowers-level impact against this defense.

When it’s not Fannin, the Browns will look to KC Concepcion Jr., the rookie wide receiver from Texas A&M. Getting him the ball in space is a primary focus of Cleveland’s offense.

Jerry Jeudy and Denzel Boston are the other primary receiving threats. Jeudy is a great route runner against zone coverage and knows how to find open space. He is complemented by Boston, who brings physical size, the ability to beat press-man coverage, and the talent to make contested catches.

The Saints will have to generate pressure on the quarterback, regardless of who is under center.

Playing against an offense that has allowed 33 sacks this season, while having Chase Young, one of the league’s sack leaders on your defensive unit, should make the coaching staff very excited.

Stop the run and generate pressure. Doing those two things will help a secondary that has been looking to return to its top-10 form from a season ago.

But stopping the run is a lot easier said than done for this squad.

The Saints are currently allowing 139 rushing yards per game, ranking 29th in the league, and the answers to fixing this run defense may not be found in 2026.

Hopefully, this game can ignite a renaissance of sorts for the Saints’ rushing defense.

How do you think the Saints will match up against the Browns defensively? Do you expect the Saints to have an edge when their defense is playing against Cleveland’s backup quarterback?

item.title: The Jaguars look like one of the NFL’s elite teams, and the best is yet to come
item.description: The Jags look great, and the rest of the AFC has been put on notice.
item.content:encoded:
Early in the second quarter of Thursday night’s game between the visiting Jacksonville Jaguars and the Baltimore Ravens, the home team had Trevor Lawrence and company in a precarious position, thanks in large part to Kyle Hamilton. After a punt pinned Jacksonville deep in their own territory, a tremendous individual tackle from Hamilton on running back Bhayshul Tuten pushed the Jaguars back to their own 1-yard line, and after a short run, the visitors faced 3rd and 7 on their own 7-yard line.

Hamilton looked poised to deliver another big play, lining up in the A-gap before the snap. A stop here would force Jacksonville to punt in a game the Jaguars led 10-3, and the ensuing field position might be enough to give the depleted Baltimore offense a chance to tie the game.

At the snap, Lawrence looked quickly to his left and Parker Washington near the first-down marker. But Hamilton, instead of blitzing, had dropped into coverage to take that read away from Lawrence.

The quarterback quickly reset, hit Jakobi Meyers on a deeper in-cut to move the chains, finding an answer for what Baltimore and Hamilton threw at him.

Final score: Jacksonville 33, Baltimore 10.

One more example of Lawrence and the Jaguars finding an answer for what teams have thrown at them so far this season.

The win moved Jacksonville to 6-2 on the season, four games clear of the Houston Texans and the Indianapolis Colts in the win column in the AFC South. A division title seems all but assured at this point, with the Colts likely finishing off a fire sale ahead of Tuesday’s NFL trade deadline and the Texans facing six of their last ten games on the road. In fact at least one playoff simulator, from The Athletic, gives the Jaguars a 98% chance of making the playoffs (and a 71% chance of hosting a Wild Card game as a division winner), and Jacksonville has the league’s easiest remaining schedule, with just three games against teams with winning records left on the slate.

However, there are a few bits of evidence one can point to that illustrate that the Jaguars are poised for something much, much more than a division title.

To start, Jacksonville’s 33-10 win over Baltimore came on the heels of a 42-7 win over the Colts in Week 8, the biggest scoring margin in a game this season. While both of those teams are reeling, those games are part of the reason why the Jaguars lead the NFL in scoring differential (+108). That is 50 points better than any other team (the San Francisco 49ers are second with a +58 scoring differential. The Jaguars have won four games by 21 points or more — a 24-point win over the Cleveland Browns and a 29-point win over the New England Patriots, in addition to the wins the last two weeks over Indianapolis and Baltimore.

No other team has more than one such victory.

Jacksonville also leads the NFL in turnover margin, at +9 on the year. And while much has been said and written about what Brian Flores and the Minnesota Vikings are doing on defense, the Jaguars are right behind them when it comes to scoring defense. Minnesota leads the way, allowing just 13.3 points per game, but Jacksonville is second in that statistic, giving up just 15.1 points per game this year.

But wait, there’s more.

Looking at Adjusted Net Yards per Attempt (ANY/A) value on both sides of the ball, as our friend Justis Mosqueda does each week, the Jaguars stand out as the best team in the AFC, and one of the best teams in the NFL:

And if you look at “Team Tiers” as measured by RBSDM, which examines Expected Points Added on both offense and defense, the Jaguars are certainly in a class by themselves in the AFC, and are side-by-side with the NFC’s best. This is after Week 8

And here is that graphic updated after Thursday night’s blowout of the Ravens:

The difference is subtle, but thanks to what the Jaguars defense did against Joe Fagnano, Jacksonville inched ahead of the 49ers in this metric.

Certainly, a big part of the story is Lawrence. As illustrated by Mosqueda’s ANY/A value, the Jaguars offense is among the league’s best passing games. The Jacksonville quarterback, as illustrated in the start to this piece, has found many answers this season. He has completed 65.2% of his passes for 1,932 yards and 18 touchdowns — against only four interceptions — and he leads all NFL passers in ANY/A with a mark of 8.5, ahead of Brock Purdy’s 8.4 and Jared Goff’s 8.0.

In addition, Lawrence also leads the league in NFL Passer Rating (111.7), Adjusted Yards per Attempt (9.4), and touchdown percentage (8%). He is also third in the NFL in EPA/dropback, behind only Josh Allen and Purdy.

It is at this point that we feel compelled to mention that Lawrence is currently fourth in MVP odds at +600 according to FanDuel, behind Allen (+160), Joe Burrow (+450), and Purdy (+550). You know, for research and evidentiary purposes …

But another part of this story is Liam Coen. Since taking over in Jacksonville, Coen and the Jaguars are 19-6, good for a winning percentage of .750. While Coen’s start last year was rather rocky — and we are not referring to the awkward “Duval” chant at his introductory press conference but rather the Jaguars’ 4-3 start to the year — since Jacksonville’s bye week a season ago the Jaguars are 15-3.

That also stands out.

Speaking after the win Thursday night, Lawrence credited the team’s ability to start fast, and not let up.

“It’s just guys being ready to play from the jump,” said Lawrence. “I’ve been on teams before where it’s like we don’t necessarily start as fast and we play better in the second half or whatever. This team, we’re just ready to go from the jump. It’s something that I think is really important not to get yourself in a hole early, and that’s something that we’ve done a good job of.”

At the NFL’s midway point, Coen and company have found all the answers they have needed, placing themselves among the league’s elite.

And putting the Jaguars on a path to even bigger things in January, and beyond.

item.title: 3 Titans players who need to play more after the bye week
item.description: Identifying three Tennessee Titans players who need to play more in Week 10 following the Week 9 bye.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans are taking a strong offensive performance in Week 8 against the Cincinnati Bengals into a Week 9 bye. Quarterback Cam Ward played the best game of his career, his first-ever 300 yard showing. Head coach Robert Saleh and staff must reflect over the bye week on necessary changes, starting with the Jacksonville Jaguars game in Week 10.

We’ve particularly identified three Titans players who need to be more involved following this weekend’s bye-week.

TE Gunnar Helm

Offensive coordinator Brian Daboll finally involved sophomore tight end Gunnar Helm in the passing attack in Week 8 and it paid dividends. Helm posted a career-high 76 receiving yards via five catches. Ward looked so comfortable targeting his reliable tight end. It was a sophomore breakout performance, and Daboll needs to ensure his momentum continues moving forward.

WR Chimere Dike

Speaking of sophomore breakouts in the passing game, Chimere Dike enjoyed one of his own versus the Bengals. The speedy special teams ace reminded the coaching staff that he’s also very useful on offense. Dike recorded five receptions for a season-high 71 yards and a touchdown. Daboll needs to continue getting him snaps on offense, even at the expense of Wan’Dale Robinson and Calvin Ridley.

CB Alontae Taylor

After benching Alontae Taylor in Week 5, his name has been mentioned in various trade-rumor articles. Trading him would be pretty complicated given they just signed him to a three-year, $58 million contract earlier this offseason. Anything is possible, but his contract isn’t exactly trade-friendly given its newness. Taylor played well at nickel corner against the Bengals after Marcus Harris got hurt. The Titans probably have to keep him in that position versus the Jaguars in Week 10.

item.title: Ravens Report Card, Week 9: More dreadful offensive play leading to a lopsided loss
item.description: The Baltimore Ravens were defeated handedly by the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday night, 33-10. It marked the team’s fourth straight loss and third consecutive defeat by 20+ points, representing a rock-bottom moment for the Ravens. Here are report card grades for Ravens’ position groups from another merciless loss in Week 9. Quarterback: F Joe Fagnano […]
item.content:encoded:
The Baltimore Ravens were defeated handedly by the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday night, 33-10. It marked the team’s fourth straight loss and third consecutive defeat by 20+ points, representing a rock-bottom moment for the Ravens. Here are report card grades for Ravens’ position groups from another merciless loss in Week 9.

Quarterback: F

Joe Fagnano had a few factors working against him in this game: he was playing through an ankle injury, had only a few days of preparation, and was facing a talented Jaguars’ defense. Nevertheless, he struggled mightily in his first career NFL start. Fagnano completed 10-of-18 passes for just 60 yards and was intercepted twice. To what extent Fagnano was limited by his ankle is unknown, but the Ravens clearly did not trust him to attempt passes more than a few yards downfield. While Fagnano was great in the preseason, a high-stakes regular season contest is clearly a different ball game for an undrafted rookie quarterback.

Running Back: C+

Derrick Henry had another inefficient rushing game, totaling 57 yards on 17 carries with a longest run of only eight yards. Henry ran hard and took on a number of wildcat snaps, but once again there was little running room to be found behind the offensive line. Justice Hill managed to break free for a long 65-yard rushing touchdown late in the game, giving the Ravens at least one notable offensive highlight. Hill finished with 92 scrimmage yards.

Wide Receiver: C-

It’s hard to knock the Ravens’ wide receivers too much given the dire state of the team’s passing attack. With Fagnano attempting few if any downfield throws, there was no chance of the wideouts doing significant damage in this game. Zay Flowers caught three passes and gained only six yards and rushed three times for 17 yards. His body language appeared deflated in the second half. Rashod Bateman and LaJohntay Wester each had once catch as well for minimal impact.

Tight End: D

Mark Andrews was the team’s leading receiver on the night with just two grabs for 19 yards. His costly miscues outweighed any impact as a pass-catcher or blocker, though. Andrews was flagged for another false start, which is a weekly occurrence now, and fumbled a snap on a fourth-and-one conversion attempt. Matthew Hibner was targeted twice and made one catch for five yards. He dropped a would-be long first down conversion, although the ball was tipped and appeared to alter the trajectory of the pass — but it still hit him in the hands. Josh Cuevas was not targeted but was flagged for a penalty.

Offensive Line: D+

Aside from Hill’s one long 65-yard run in the second half, the Ravens were once again unable to open up many rushing lanes up front. Fagnano was only sacked once and hit four times, but he didn’t drop back in the pocket very often anyways. It was a positive to have Vega Ioane back in the lineup at right guard, which allowed the Ravens to finally play a full game with their ideal five-man group together. Unfortunately, the results were not notable. Ronnie Stanley was flagged for another pre-snap penalty, his fifth flag in the last two weeks.

Defensive Line: C

The Ravens did a great job defending the run up front. Jacksonville’s top two rushers, Byshaul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr., combined for 22 carries and gained 48 yards. They each scored a touchdown, but their scores came on short yardage runs in the red zone. Unfortunately, the Ravens got very little pressure through the interior on Trevor Lawrence. On the bright side, Nnamdi Madubuike had two deflected passes (although he was flagged for a costly offside penalty on fourth down) and Broderick Washington had a pass breakup. Madubuike had the team’s only quarterback hit. Travis Jones played strong as well and recorded a tackle for loss.

Edge Rusher: D+

The edge rushers were a positive factor against the run as well, setting the edge and preventing explosive outside rushes. However, they were almost a complete no show in the pass rushing department. Not a single edge defender recorded a sack, quarterback hit or tackle for loss. Trey Hendrickson is clearly bothered by his finger injury, but it would still be nice to see him start making impact plays more consistently. Mike Green had a nice run stop at the line of scrimmage, but the Ravens need him to get after the quarterback. Without Tavius Robinson, this group has left much to be desired over the last few weeks.

Linebacker: B-

Roquan Smith had a team-leading eight tackles and made a strong stop at the goal line on the Jaguars’ opening drive. In pass coverage, Smith appears out of place over the middle of the field too often. Trenton Simpson had six tackles, and Teddye Buchanan recovered a fumble in the second half along with a good play against the run too.

Cornerback: D+

The hits keep on coming for Marlon Humphrey, who was beaten for a long 52-yard reception within the first few plays of the game. On that play, the Ravens had the Jaguars dead to rights, but Humphrey got lost and allowed a backup tight end to get behind him. He had two pass breakups later in the game. With Nate Wiggins sidelined, Chidobe Awuzie got the start and had one tackle. Awuzie was beaten at least once by Jakobi Meyers and appeared to whiff on a tackle in space. As a whole, the Ravens’ corners continue to be far too inconsistent and prone to coverage lapses.

Safety: C–

Kyle Hamilton exited the game in the second half with a hip injury and did not return. Prior to that, he was one of the team’s lone bright spots, blowing up a run that nearly resulted in a safety and recording a pass breakup that should have been picked off. Malaki Starks was beaten badly by Parker Washington in the slot for a long 50-yard touchdown reception. Starks should not have been in one-on-one coverage against Washington, but it was a reminder of his limitations as a coverage player. He did redeem himself with a forced fumble on Travis Hunter later in the game.

Special Teams: C+

Jake Moody made a good first impression as the Ravens’ new kicker, nailing a 53-yard attempt in the first quarter. Ryan Eckley had five punts with three inside the 20-yard line and a longest of 55 yards. In the punt return game, Wester returned only one try and gained 10 yards. Given their offensive limitations right now, the Ravens badly need some splash special teams plays to win and they aren’t getting them.

item.title: The Rams officially going with two kickers, sign Joshua Karty
item.description: The Los Angeles Rams are trying to get their special teams right, it’s been their story all year, and more news
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams rolled with two kickers in Week 8, and they are doing it again as they made it official before Week 9 by signing Joshua Karty and Brandon McManus to their roster. Karty is expected to handle kickoffs, while McManus will handle field goals.

Karty botched two kickoffs last week by not hitting them into the landing zone, setting up the opponent at the 40-yard line due to penalty. McManus has been flawless on his attempts since joining the Rams. He’s been fine, but the team hasn’t seen if McManus can handle a high-pressure kick such as a game winning one.

All things come in time, the Rams will find out if McManus can handle it or not, they’ll also see if Karty can improve, but their kicking position is still a question mark despite all their changes. It’s clear that as the Rams continue to make changes, they don’t exactly know what they are doing. But they are trying. Points for trying. Then again, points for trying, doesn’t always lead to points on the field.

Rams sign Joshua Karty to active roster and bring back former 3rd-round CB (ramswire)

“The kicking carousel continues to spin for the Los Angeles Rams. On Thursday, the Rams announced they have signed Joshua Karty from the practice squad to the 53-man roster, giving them two kickers on the active roster; Brandon McManus is the other.

Additionally, the team reunited with cornerback David Long Jr., who Los Angeles drafted in the third round back in 2019. Long has been signed to the practice squad, taking the spot vacated by Karty’s promotion.

It’s surprising that the Rams signed Karty to the 53-man roster after elevating him for the first time last week. They could have used a temporary elevation on him twice more, but perhaps they want to reserve their practice squad promotions for players at another position.“

Rams Midweek Report: A Concerning Trend on Offense, Matthew Stafford’s Elbow, and Trade Buzz (si.com)

“There is certainly some context to that as Davante Adams and Puka Nacua have each missed games. Terrance Ferguson has also been out since Week 3. At the same time, the Rams haven’t pushed the ball down the field very often. 

Through eight weeks this season, the Rams’ passing game has an explosive play rate of just 4.1 percent. At this point last year, the passing game had an explosive play rate of 17.5 percent and it was 18.2 percent for the season. 

The passing game is less than one-fourth as explosive as it was last year. That lack of explosiveness certainly helps explain some of the Rams’ troubles scoring consistently. Picking up yards hasn’t been an issue. The Rams also rank sixth in touchdown rate once they get into the red zone.“

Commanders Daily: The Rams Have More Than Film on Jayden Daniels (si.com)

“When asked if Kingsbury and Johnson could share their knowledge of Washington’s personnel with the Rams’ defense, Blough’s response was direct: “I think so. I think everybody in every role shares information. And yeah, they certainly know our guys. We know what they know about our guys, and we kind of go from there.”

There’s no getting around the fact that the Rams will come equipped with information on Washington’s strengths and tendencies from a year ago. Kingsbury and Johnson helped prepare Daniels each week, which gave them a chance to see what he handled well and what needed more work. That experience can help the Rams make sense of what they’re seeing from him in Blough’s offense now. They will certainly know the assistant that Blough was; hell, they’ll know Dan Quinn even better. That’s the type of familiarity Washington’s staff will need to account for.“

Rams can’t waste any more time achieving a sustainable offense (ramblinfan)

“Complicating the matter is the fact that injuries are depleting the team. The Rams have played most of the season without up-and-coming tight end Terrance Ferguson. Now Davante Adams is on injured reserve. And much to fans’ horror, even durable Matthew Stafford is suffering from arm soreness.

LA is facing a midseason crisis. Yes, the offense can gain yards and remains one of the NFL’s best. But it lags at 10th place in scoring. The Rams haven’t converted moving the football into points on the scoreboard.

The strategy that has carried the offense to Week 9 won’t work going forward. The strain on the few entrusted playmakers is taking its toll.“

Commanders defense faces major challenge in Rams WR Puka Nacua (sports.yahoo)

“Not only is Nacua very talented, but Rams head coach Sean McVay really moves Nacua around. “Oh, they do a great job the way they move him; the way they utilize him,” Jones said. “He’s in the run game, because he is physical,” Jones said. The Rams run the ball well, and the second-level blocking of Nacua has certainly helped Rams ball carriers. In addition, the Rams occasionally will hand off the ball to Nacua. In 2025, he ran ten times for 105 yards and five rushing first downs.

But make no mistake, Nacua is still one of the real workhorses in the NFL. He hurts opposing defenses with his ability to go into the middle, catch short passes and sometimes get beat up, and sometimes break free for larger yardage. Though Nacua was injured in the opener and missed the next two games, he has still collected 56 receptions, 26 receiving first downs and three touchdowns.“

Washington Commanders vs. Los Angeles Rams: 3 reasons for optimism (sports.yahoo)

“A steady ground game could create more manageable third downs and make play-action more effective. It would also give Washington a way to extend possessions and limit opportunities for Matthew Stafford and the Rams’ offense.

Washington’s defense is showing it can produce game-changing plays

The Commanders’ defense delivered a performance against Philadelphia that offers encouragement heading into a tougher assignment. They recorded five sacks, including one that produced a fumble recovery deep in Eagles territory. Rasul Douglas also intercepted a fourth-down pass, helping the Commanders finish a game in which they scored 27 unanswered points.“

LA Rams vs Washington Commanders: Three Matchups to Watch (sports.yahoo)

“Jayden Daniels is playing really well over the last two weeks, ranking top ten in multiple categories and leading the league with zero turnovers. Through five games, he has thrown for 976 yards, six touchdowns, and zero interceptions on a 62.8% completion rate — and he has added 236 rushing yards and two scores on the ground. Daniels was 16-of-29 for 217 yards in the Sunday night win over Philadelphia, and he followed a 199 passing yard, 103 rushing yard, two score performance from week five with that gritty showing.

Now he faces a Los Angeles Rams defense that will test whether the momentum is real. The Rams have shown they can pressure the quarterback and take away one side of the field, so Daniels’ ability to extend plays, work through progressions, and hit the deep ball will all be on display.“

Commanders vs Rams predictions, picks, odds for NFL Week 9 game Sunday (azcentral)

“Which team has the best chance to win the game according to NFL Week 9 win probabilities?

Check out The Arizona Republic’s score projection for the Sunday football game, as well as Rams vs. Commanders picks, odds and win chances for the NFL Week 9 game, which can be seen at 11 a.m. MST on FOX (stream with FUBO).“

Rams pass rush poses major test for Commanders (cbssports)

“Even absent Garrett, with Donald drawing attention in the middle, Young has been able to flourish. He’s got 4 1/2 sacks this season.

“When you allocate resources to one elite premium player, he’s gonna get a one-on-one matchup,” Blough said. “We gotta be able to win on the perimeter. And he’s elite pass rusher, really good bull rush in this league and we gotta be ready for him.”

While Young provides a challenge on the edge, Donald, who doesn’t have a sack this season, still can have a massive impact on how an opposing offense operates with an interior rush.“

item.title: Lions vs. Dolphins 5 Qs preview: Is Miami mirroring Detroit’s 2021 culture rebuild?
item.description: Here’s our Q&A preview with Phinsider about this Week 9 matchup between the Detroit Lions and Miami Dolphins.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions head to South Beach for a Week 9 interconference matchup against a young, rebuilding Miami Dolphins team.

We had the pleasure of connecting with Kevin Nogle, the Managing Editor of Phinsider to give us some insight into this Miami team ahead of Sunday’s kickoff. We learned about the local sentiment surrounding head coach Jeff Hafley’s foundational reset, how offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik is tailoring the offense to quarterback Malik Willis, and how Ollie Gordon is handling the backfield workload in De’Von Achane’s absence—plus what Miami needs to do to keep pace with Detroit’s offense.

1. Miami arguably made more changes to their organization than any other team in the NFL this offseason. New head coach, new quarterback, the changing out of long-tenured skill position players—it was a massive overhaul in South Beach. 

Although the Dolphins are off to a 1-6 start, how much of that was expected from a team that underwent so many changes this offseason? It’s early, but do you get the sense that new head coach Jeff Hafley is the right guy for this rebuild?

This year is about setting up the franchise for the future, and while losses are never fun, the struggles were expected. This is the league’s youngest team, and they are facing a steep learning curve. Miami has 14 rookies on the roster, plus another seven first-year players. This is clearly a reset of the team’s foundation, and there will be growing pains. 

The Dolphins’ schedule has also been brutal this year. They started the year against the Las Vegas Raiders, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs, and Minnesota Vikings, not facing a team that had a loss until Week 5 against the Cincinnati Bengals, who were 2-2 coming into that game. Through Week 8, Miami has faced the league’s toughest schedule, with a combined opponent winning percentage of .589. The schedule is not an excuse, but with such a young team, it is another variable to consider. 

Obviously, things can change, but Hafley has instilled confidence in the fanbase so far. The Mike McDaniel era had some fun moments, but it quickly fell apart and the team never adjusted (and McDaniel still does not seem to have made adjustments as the Los Angeles Chargers struggle this year). I think Hafley’s focus on making the Dolphins physical, allowing the younger players to gain experience, and the team’s ability to make adjustments, learn from mistakes, and continue to fight even in losing situations indicate he is the right guy for this role. Lions fans saw Dan Campbell build a culture out of tough losses back in 2021; that is exactly the phase Hafley and the Dolphins are in right now. 

2. From the outside looking in, Malik Willis was dropped into a tough situation given the pieces around him in the offense—and it looks like, predictably, the passing game has struggled so far. The Dolphins rank 26th in passing DVOA and EPA/pass. 

How has Bobby Slowik tried to tailor this offense to Willis’ strengths? What’s working, what’s not working, and how much of that is related to a new quarterback in a new system versus the lack of talent personnel-wise?

I think we are starting to see Willis find some comfort in the offensive system, and he is starting to play better. Despite being a third-round pick in 2022, Willis has played in only 29 career games, starting just 13. He is a league veteran but really has the starting experience of a rookie. At times, he still seems bothered by the speed of the game, but the experience he is getting this year is already making a difference in his play. 

I think one of the biggest issues we have seen from Willis is a desire to be a pocket passer. He stays in the pocket longer than he should, trying to find the perfect pass rather than taking something shorter or throwing the ball away to avoid a sack. The offensive line is not doing him any favors, but he has taken multiple sacks by running out of bounds instead of throwing the ball away. He seemed to want to avoid using his legs, but has opened up that part of his game in the last couple of weeks. 

Slowik, like McDaniel before him, has an offensive system built on quarterback accuracy and timing. He uses bootlegs, run-pass options, and play-action passes to get Willis out of the pocket and seeing open receivers. They also seem to be using some half-field concepts, keeping Willis looking in one area and working from deep to shallow rather than having him search the entire field for receivers. 

The youth on the roster – especially with wide receivers Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell, and Kevin Coleman Jr. – do not always create separation, and drops have also been an issue. When the primary target is not open on time, a young quarterback hesitates, and behind an evolving offensive line, hesitation leads to sacks. That all relates back to the discussion of Miami’s reset this year. The potential for talent is on Miami’s roster, but they still need to grow individually and together. The coaching staff is clearly working on the balance between youth and system – relying on a more basic system as the players learn. 

3. Losing De’Von Achane in the first month of the season felt especially cruel for this offense that was already so limited on difference makers. The Dolphins rank 9th in EPA/rush (-0.03) but rank near the bottom of the league in rush success rate (26th) and rush DVOA (26th), suggesting that their run game is a boom-or-bust attack. 

Is that a fair assessment of Ollie Gordon’s performance this year? The Dolphins also rank 26th in stuffed rate (22.8%) which is the percentage of runs that earn zero or negative yards. Are those stuffed runs more of an indictment of the offensive line or the coaching/play calling?

That seems like a fair assessment. Gordon has been a lot of fun to watch as he breaks out this year, but he is a power-back who works extremely well as a change-of-pace option behind Achane. When he finds space, he is able to break it for a big gain, but it really is boom or bust on each run.

Part of that is Gordon and his abilities. Part of that is the offensive line finding space to get him free. And part of that is opposing defenses planning to stop the run. Miami has had success this year, averaging 131 rushing yards per game, and they have topped 100 yards in five of seven games, including one game over 150 yards and another over 200 yards. They also have two games with 74 yards rushing each. Boom or bust.

The offensive line—especially last week with Kadyn Proctor out with a concussion—still has work to do to come together as a unit. 

I think play calling is part of it, but not necessarily because the plays are wrong, but rather because the player is wrong. The rushing attack was built for Achane’s skill set, complemented by Gordon. Now, it is a Gordon-led unit and some of the designs are clearly meant for Achane’s speed over Gordon’s power. We have seen that evolve as Slowik has adjusted to Gordon, but there is an obvious difference between the two players and there will likely be a boom or bust aspect to the Dolphins’ ground game all season. The outside zone, stretch concepts were designed for Achane’s elite sideline-to-sideline track speed. Gordon is a one-cut, downhill runner. The Dolphins have pivoted to more gap and inside-zone looks to match Gordon’s style, but until defenses are forced to back out of the box, stops will linger. 

4. Hafley brings his decades of experience coaching defense to Miami, and the numbers related to personnel deployment and coverage usage are pretty interesting through eight weeks. Miami lines up in base personnel 51.7% of snaps, second-most in the NFL, and they’re utilizing zone coverage 78.8% of the time (10th in the NFL).

How much of these numbers overlap with the talent available on the current roster? In other words, does it feel like Hafley’s trying to put his players in the best spots to succeed? Numbers suggest the run defense is bordering on being a top-10 unit, but the pass defense might be the worst in the league. Do those numbers tell the whole story?

Hafley definitely relies on base defense and he expects his front four to create pressure, rather than relying on the blitz—especially when compared to someone like Brian Flores, a former Dolphins head coach, and his blitz heavy defense. Hafley expects the pressure to come from the front four, allowing him to keep additional players back in coverage or focused on the run. It has been successful—at least as successful as can be expected with the younger players executing on the field. 

The run defense has been strong for much of the year. There have been mistakes, especially when an edge rusher bites on a play action, chasing the quarterback and failing to set the edge or runs right past the ball carrier, but overall, they are doing well against the run. Of course, I say all of that knowing full well Jahmyr Gibbs is second in the league in rushing and is averaging nearly five-yards-per-carry, so the pressure is on the defense to continue to find success this week.

Does the contrast between the pass defense and the run defense tell the entire story? Not necessarily. The heavy zone scheme with the younger defensive backs is designed to prevent explosive, 60+ yard plays. That is allowing for short and intermediate routes to pick apart defenses (especially when Miami struggles to cover tight ends. Good thing the Lions are not bringing a top-tier tight end into this game, right?!?). Add in that Miami has been playing from behind for much of the year, and the short, possession passing game has been highly effective.

I do think Hafley is keeping his defensive calls a little more basic than maybe we will see from him in the next few years, allowing the foundation to be set before he starts building off of it. The Dolphins have stressed that they expect to build for the future through the draft and grow the team from within. If they stick to that plan, I think you will see both the offense and defense evolve as the players grow and Miami moves from a roster dominated by rookies to one with veterans hitting their prime supported by key rookies each year. 

5. The Dolphins opened as 7-point home underdogs over at FanDuel Sportsbook heading into this Week 9 matchup against the Lions. What’s one thing you want to see, what’s one thing you need to see, and one thing you’re sure you’ll see happen in this matchup between the Lions and Dolphins on Sunday afternoon?

I want to see the offense be aggressive and take shots downfield. The Lions are allowing 276 yards per game through the air, and they are banged up. Let Willis test them early, get Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell into the game, and use the play-action to create opportunities. The Dolphins need to come into this game feeling like they have to win in a shoot-out. If they are aggressive on offense, maybe they can catch the Lions a little flat-footed at the start.

I need to see the Dolphins continue to make adjustments week-to-week, correct mistakes from the last game, and grow as a unit. That will be true throughout this season. Continued growth week to week is important and seeing the team not make the same mistakes over and over will continue to keep Dolphins fans confident the team is headed in the right direction.

I am sure I will see the Dolphins compete in this game and play hard through the fourth quarter. They may not be biting kneecaps (I love Dan Campbell and miss him in Miami), but they should be physical and give it everything they have on every down. I am also sure I will see Campbell continue to be aggressive on third- and fourth-down. The Dolphins have allowed over 50 percent conversion for opposing offenses on third down this year. They have to expect the Lions to attack on third down, and then attack again on fourth down. 

The Lions are coming into this game as the better team. They should leave Miami having proven they are the better team. But, if Miami executes well, they can at least stand toe-to-toe with Detroit throughout the game, take the punches, and fight through the final bell. Really, the Dolphins have the ability to be the 2021 Lions – growing with a first-year head coach, taking a bad season and turning it into the foundation for a brighter future. If Miami can follow the same pathway as the Lions, this would be a successful rebuild.
