item.title: Chiefs-Jets: 5 Things to Watch in Week 9 matchup
item.description: What to keep an eye on when Kansas City squares up with New York on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The Kansas City Chiefs (5-2) will take on the (2-6) New York Jets Sunday afternoon in an AFC showdown. The game kicks off at 12:00 PM Arrowhead time and will be broadcast on CBS.

The Chiefs, losers of two straight, lost a heartbreaker last week, 28-24 to the Denver Broncos. The Chiefs controlled most of the game, but a fourth-quarter offensive meltdown and major defensive breakdowns let the Broncos snatch a late victory.

The Jets also lost last week, falling to the Las Vegas Raiders 38-33. With three straight losses, the Jets are among the bottom dwellers in the AFC, despite having a roster with quality talent in multiple critical positions.

The Chiefs need a win to keep pace in the AFC standings, while the Jets are seeking a signature win for second-year head coach Aaron Glenn:

Here are five things to watch

1. Emmett Johnson’s usage

This season, Johnson has shown flashes of the player he can become, but this week against Denver, he exploded onto the scene with a massive game. With 145 all-purpose yards and a touchdown, he was voted NFL Rookie of the Week.

Johnson had been quiet up to this point in terms of production, but his ability to break tackles had drawn attention and was on full display as he ran all over the Denver defense.

Johnson is the Chiefs’ third-leading receiver behind only Travis Kelce and Rashee Rice, ahead of players like Xavier Worthy and Noah Gray. The Chiefs offense needs help not only finding explosive playmakers, but also finding consistent playmakers.

Johnson can be both, and the Chiefs should get him the ball more often.

2. Stuffing Braelon Allen

Jets star running back Breece Hall was a full participant in Thursday’s practice after being on the Reserve/Injured list since Week 3. The Jets’ run game didn’t skip a step, and his backup Braelon Allen has stepped in and stepped up.

Allen has rushed for over 100 yards in three of his last four games and has been the driving force in New York’s offense.

Allen is poised for a bright career, but Kansas City should be able to stop him. The Chiefs’ defense currently ranks 8th in the NFL in rushing yards allowed per game at 96.3. Linebacker Nick Bolton is tied for 10th in the NFL this season with 68 total tackles and will play arguably the biggest role in stopping Allen on Sunday.

Allen may be young, but Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo made sure to give him his due in Thursday’s media availability.

I think he looks (Ravens RB) Derrick Henry-ish to me sometimes,“ Spags described Allen. ”He’s a big guy. So, we’ve got to be on point tackling.”

If Hall does indeed return, it will be interesting to see how the Jets divide their touches against the Chiefs.

3. Rookie edge rushers

This week will feature two of the NFL’s premier rookie pass rushers.

The Jets defense will feature No. 2 overall draft pick David Bailey coming off the edge, while the Chiefs more so rotate in second-round pick R Mason Thomas.

Bailey was the cream of the crop for pass rushers in this past year’s draft and is already the Jets’ best pass rusher, with 5.5 sacks so far this season. Bailey (groin) missed last week with an injury, but he practiced in full on Thursday and is trending toward playing Sunday.

Bailey will draw most of the headlines, but the Chiefs have their own young, budding pass rusher.

While Thomas has been a rotational player for the Chiefs so far this season, he has been productive and disruptive on the snaps he has seen.

The Chiefs only have nine sacks as a team so far this season, and defensive end George Karlaftis is the only player with more than one. Thomas has seen a slight dip in snaps the last two weeks, but the Chiefs should look to up his pass-rush looks, especially on obvious passing downs.

Both offensive lines will have their work cut out, and each rookie rusher can change the game for their team.

4. Field Goal unit

At this point in the season, it is not a matter of whether Harrison Butker will miss a kick; it is a matter of when, and that thought should linger in the Chiefs’ minds when they get into fourth-down situations across midfield.

Butker missed a critical kick late in the game in Denver, allowing the Broncos to turn around and quickly take the late lead. Many suspected it could be the end of Butker in Kansas City, but this week the Chiefs coaching staff stood behind their long-time kicker.

“You exhaust every possibility to get this guy right, Toub told reporters on Thursday. ”And that’s what we’re doing right now. We’re not just going to pull the plug.”

“Butker’s our kicker,” Toub continued. ‘He’s on our team, and we’re paying Butker. And Butker has won a lot of football games for us. Butker is a champion. And he deserves the right to be exhausted on this thing, and we’re going to exhaust every possibility with him.”

Regardless of the confidence, fourth-down situations will get even more interesting once the Chiefs get past midfield. I would expect to see the Chiefs punt in fourth-and-long situations this week if they do get into what was once Butker’s range. The team ranks 17th in the league with a 53.85% conversion rate on fourth down, and it will be interesting if they decide to attack these situations moving forward.

5. A potential quarterback sneak?

Short-yardage ineptitude led to disaster for the Chiefs’ offense last week, and this week speculation rose about an ongoing issue.

Mahomes has not run a quarterback sneak since a freak injury in October 2019, and while the team has run it with other players taking the snap, they haven’t shown the look in quite some time.

In Denver, the Chiefs failed on three straight snaps from the one-yard line, and this week both Mahomes and Reid were questioned about the willingness to run a quarterback sneak.

The Chiefs brass did their best to dispel the notion that they were afraid to let Mahomes sneak the ball in short-yardage situations, but their actions say otherwise.

An early November matchup against the Jets might not be the time for Mahomes to reintroduce the quarterback sneak, but it will be worth watching how the Chiefs handle short-yardage situations.

item.title: Cowboys at Colts: Offensive, defensive impact players in Week 9
item.description: Two Cowboys who should have a big impact on Sunday
item.content:encoded:
Whether it’s due to talent or circumstances, certain players impact the game more than others week in and week out. The Dallas Cowboys have several such players who can help turn the tide at any moment in any given game. To hopefully get their season back on track and start stacking some wins together, they need these players to step up now more than ever.

In the Week 9 matchup with the Indianapolis Colts we believe the Cowboys have a player on each side of the ball who will impact the game in a big way in this week, and we discuss why these two individuals should help sway the game in the Cowboys favor.

Offense – RB Javonte Williams

The offensive game plan and play-calling for Brian Schottenheimer should be an easy one this week, run the ball early and often. The Indianapolis Colts currently ranked 27th in the league in run defense, allowing 131.8 rushing yards per game.

That should equate to a big game for Javonte Williams, and possibly Tyler Goodson as well. These two combined for nearly 200 total rushing yards a couple weeks ago against the Eagles and could duplicate that success in this Week 9 matchup with the Colts.

We expect No. 33 to have a huge impact on the outcome of the game and predict he’ll have his second 100+ rushing yard performance of the season. This, of course, all hinges on how the offensive line performs. They’ve been a little hit and miss all season, but are at their best when run blocking. If everything comes together and plays out as we expect, Dallas’ run game should propel them to victory this week.

Defense – DT Quinnen Williams

Quinnen Williams got off to somewhat of a slow start to the 2026 season, but has recently been playing at an elite level. He completely dominated in what was unfortunately a losing effort last week against the Arizona Cardinals, collecting a couple of QB sacks. He dominate once again in this Week 9 matchup with the Indianapolis Colts, whose offensive line has been struggling, especially along the interior.

Williams should be licking his chops for this matchup. We fully expect him to test the Colts rookie LG Jalen Farmer, a fourth-round pick this year, early and often. He replaced All-Pro Quenton Nelson after he was traded to the Seattle Seahawks a few weeks ago. This is a battle No. 92 should be able to easily exploit to his advantage, and in so doing, help secure the “W” for the Cowboys.

item.title: Reviewing Steelers narratives at the bye week: Elite defense? Top-5 O-line?
item.description: Breaking down the 12 biggest Steelers storylines at midseason.
item.content:encoded:
As the Steelers enter a Week 9 bye, the midseason break from Pittsburgh football presents a perfect opportunity to look at the big picture of the team as the crucial second half of the season approaches.

At 6-2 and currently on a four-game winning streak, it’s fair to say the Steelers might be overhyped in some areas. But every fanbase has its doubters, and there might be too much doom and gloom when it comes to some storylines, as well.

As a result, this week Steelers Read & React will be taking a look at the 12 biggest Steelers narratives at midseason. Which ones are real? Which ones are stretching the truth? Is it just too early to tell with some? Find out our thoughts below, and let us know yours in the comments:

Zach Frazier is an All-Pro

RB: After a few seasons of always hovering near the top of NFL media’s top interior lineman rankings, Frazier has broken into “best center in the NFL” territory during the Steelers’ recent win streak.

Film bros love Frazier. Analytics nerds do too, with Frazier ranking first in the NFL at his position in PFF grades, with 79.5 as of this writing. And the Steelers’ line as a whole has been mauling as of late, ranking top-10 in both run success rate and lowest quarterback pressure rate so far this season. Frazier’s combination of toughness, athleticism, strength, and football IQ has been quite literally in the center of all of Pittsburgh’s recent success on offense in 2026.

Barring a big-time drop-off from Frazier and/or the Steelers’ offense in the second half of the season, a first- or second-team All-Pro seems almost guaranteed at this point for the Pittsburgh center. At the moment, he has all the media hype, and more importantly, the play to back it up.

The verdict: Absolutely.

The defense is elite

RP: I don’t want to be a downer on what has been a better first half of the season than many expected, but I will be a stickler about how readily we throw the “E” word around. The Pittsburgh defense has been stellar over the past month. It’s been mostly healthy, save for the Derrick Harmon injury and Jalen Ramsey playing through a fractured wrist. Even DeShon Elliott is back.

But I stop short of calling this unit “elite,” at least for now. For starters, just look at who they’ve played.

With the clear exception of the Bengals, and a Patriots offense that requires a lot of context when discussing whether or not they’ve been “good” this year, the Steelers haven’t exactly been playing the NFL’s top offenses. Likewise, with the exception of Joe Burrow and Drake Maye — and again, Maye has significantly rebounded in his quality of play since facing the Steelers in Week 2 — the Steelers haven’t been facing the cream of the crop under center either.

That doesn’t diminish what the Pittsburgh defense has been doing in recent weeks. Heading into the bye, the Steelers lead the NFL in sacks (26). They rank sixth in both EPA allowed per pass (-0.15) and per rush (-0.12), and are tied for the fifth-lowest average yards per carry allowed (3.6). They’ve allowed just 17 runs of 10 or more yards, tied for the eighth-fewest in the NFL. The 18 points per game they’re surrendering ranks third in the NFL, as do their 13 takeaways (seven interceptions, six fumble recoveries).

Still, it’s hard for me to declare this an “elite” defense full-throatedly without seeing them face a great offense outside of the division. Unfortunately, a look at the Steelers’ remaining schedule likely won’t give many chances for them to be tested.

Among the opponents left on Pittsburgh’s schedule, only Jacksonville (3rd), Cincinnati (6th), Houston (13th), and Carolina (14th) rank in the top half of the NFL in offensive EPA. Among those, only the Jaguars (+0.11) and the Bengals (+0.07) are generating positive EPA per play, and it should be noted that Carolina’s offense has been in free fall after a hot September.

Similarly, among the quarterbacks the Steelers have left on the schedule, only Trevor Lawrence (4th), Burrow (6th), and C.J. Stroud (10th) rank inside the top-15 passers in EPA per dropback on the season. I’ll dive a little further into what the games against these passers might tell us about the AFC playoffs in the final question of this column.

There’s also some nosiness with the Steelers current lead in sacks. While their raw total is enough to presently lead the NFL, some of the underlying metrics might indicate they’ve had some luck in that regard. The Steelers rank 26th in the NFL in pressure rate (32.6%) and just 16th in total pressures. This says to me that the Steelers might have had a knack for getting timely sacks, but they are not generating as much pressure against the pass as their sack totals might have us otherwise think. I could be overthinking things, certainly, but when paired with my nagging concern about the level of quarterback play this defense has faced, it does leave room to wonder how the defense might fare against some of the more skilled quarterbacks they’re certain to face in the playoffs.

The verdict: Incomplete. The numbers are great, and Patrick Graham is accenting the strengths of his players while limiting exposure to their weaknesses — but we need to see them against better offenses first.

T.J. Watt is back, baby

RB: T.J. Watt is back atop the NFL sacks leaderboard (tied for first with the Texans’ Will Anderson with 7.5) after a two-sack performance against the Browns on Sunday. Sure, it took him one more game to reach that number than the Texans’ star, but considering Watt is 32 and was pronounced as “washed” by a number of fans last year after logging seven sacks in 14 games, it’s good to see him back in superstar territory.

I’d argue the eye test and advanced stats still show that Watt isn’t quite the player he was in his prime. This year, his pressure rate is a very good 10.7% (that number hovered between 13.7% and 17.6% in all but one of his first six seasons) and his playing-time percentage has also dropped to what is by far a career low at 65.1% after being above 82% in all but one of his prior seasons.

However, Watt’s sack percentage has jumped up to 3.5%, on track for the third-best mark of his career, while his get-off time is currently the second-fastest of his career at 0.72 seconds on average.

The point is that the Steelers are reviving Watt’s efficiency by letting him rest far more than in past years — and it’s working just about perfectly. His $42 million cap hit this season and the next (and $46 million in 2028 but there’s an out) isn’t exactly negligible, but I don’t think you could be expecting a much better season than this from a pass-rusher of Watt’s age who has seen a downtick in production over the last two seasons.

Is Watt back? Not to his 2021 self, but I doubt any reasonable person expected that. He’s still absolutely a star.

The verdict: Not entirely, but he’s still very, very good.

The Steelers have a top-5 O-line

RP: Creating lists and ranking things is something people love to do, especially sports fans. I’m no different. Still, when you’re looking at something that’s so subjective and influenced by a wide variety of factors, finding a way to make your case can be both a thrilling and tiring experience all at once.

I’ll try to break down my analysis as simply and clearly as I can, but if you come away with a different opinion, don’t be all that surprised. There is no one perfect stat that can tell us which offensive line is the best!

Let’s start with the first criteria I considered: I wanted the 10 teams with the best EPA per rush as a starting point. I chose this because there are fewer outside factors to consider when running the ball than passing. In the passing game, EPA can be affected dramatically by the level of play by the quarterback and pass catchers. Likewise, scheme can mask how good or bad a team is at blocking by getting the ball out quickly to avoid pressures and sacks. Last year’s Steelers were a great example of this. But in the run game, the offensive line has a much more obvious influence on the overall success of the play.

As such, these were the top 10 teams in EPA/Rush in order:

  • T-Chiefs and Bills
  • T- Steelers and 49ers
  • Jacksonville
  • T-Rams and Colts
  • Buccaneers
  • T-Cowboys and Dolphins

The Steelers are within the top three in this stat, so that’s a great start for our case. But while EPA per rush has fewer outside factors than passing, it can still be influenced by the quality of the running back. An exceptional running back, like Jaylen Warren, could theoretically outperform his offensive line. Again, there is no singular stat that will provide us clarity, but I looked at two other stats with these 10 teams: average yards before contact and rushing success rate.

Starting with yards before contact, the Steelers take a big hit here. Only two of the teams in our top 10 — the Jaguars and Cowboys — don’t have a better figure in this metric. Pittsburgh actually ranks 13th in the NFL with an average of 1.25 yards before contact. This isn’t a case breaker, however. The top three teams in this regard — Ravens, Vikings, Commanders — weren’t in our original list, and all three have negative EPA per rush. Miami, Dallas, and Jacksonville all join Pittsburgh in falling outside the top-10 in this specific metric. And it should be noted that the top ranking of our initial 10 lines — Buffalo with 1.74 — is only averaging about a half yard better. This tells me that Warren boosts the performance of the Steelers’ running game, but the Pittsburgh offensive line is still getting a top-half of the league push.

The Steelers fared better when considering rushing success rate. Here they rank ninth (43.5%) in the NFL, and sixth among our initial 10 teams. The teams with a higher success rate were: the 49ers (51.8%), Rams (49.8%), Bills (48.8%), Chiefs (45.4%), and Cowboys (45.2%).

Considering just the running game, it’s clear the Steelers are in the hunt for top-five status. Now let’s try to parse out the pass-blocking. For this, I considered three metrics: average time to pressure, pressure rate, and total sacks. These metrics, of course, are not perfect. Quarterbacks can often be just as responsible for sacks and pressures as their line is — see the tweet below — and scheme and a quarterback’s own aversion to being hit can skew how quickly they get the ball out, which can mitigate pressures from an otherwise shaky line. Still, they give us some form of measurement, and we can try our best to give proper weight to each metric from there.

Considering the three metrics above, here’s how the Steelers compared:

  • Total sacks is the Steelers’ worst argument. The Colts and Bucs have the same total sacks allowed as the Steelers (23), and every other team allowed fewer.
  • The Steelers average 2.64 seconds before pressure. Five teams on our list allowed more time on average: the Bills (2.87), Dolphins (2.77), 49ers (2.76), Chiefs (2.69), and Bucs (2.66).
  • Pressure rate is where the Steelers show best, with a 29.9% rate. Only the 49ers (26.7%) and Rams (29.6%) allow a lower rate. The rest of our contenders: Bills (31.0%), Cowboys (31.9%), Chiefs (32.9%), Jaguars (34.4%), Bucs (37.2%), Dolphins (43.2%).

That’s a lot of data I’ve thrown at you, certainly. But as I consider our list of teams, I think it’s easy to eliminate the Buccaneers, Dolphins, Jaguars, and Colts from our list. Each of these units allowed higher rates of pressure than Pittsburgh as pass-blocking units, and they finished behind the Steelers in EPA per rush and rushing success rate. And it should be considered that the Colts traded away Quenton Nelson, their best offensive lineman.

So with those teams eliminated, by estimation, the six teams in the running for a top-five ranking are: the Bills, Chiefs, Cowboys, 49ers, Rams, and the Steelers.

Of those other units:

  • All five had a higher rushing success rate.
  • The Cowboys were tied with the Steelers in average yards before contact. The other four teams ranked better.
  • The Chiefs, Bills, Niners, and Rams had longer average times to pressure than Pittsburgh. The Cowboys did not.
  • Each team allowed fewer sacks than Pittsburgh, but the Steelers trailed only the Niners and Rams in pressure rate. Those two offenses both come from the Shanahan tree and involve two of the NFL’s top playcallers and designers. Take that for what you will.

The verdict: They’re currently closer to five than to one, but there’s a reasonable case to be made. At worst, they’re knocking on the door as the sixth-best line.

The Steelers’ coaching staff has been excellent

RB: I’m not implying that Mike McCarthy is the exact same coach as Mike Tomlin — not at all — but let’s be honest: The Steelers rebounding from some early ugly losses with a midseason winning streak highlighted by a statement win heading into the bye isn’t exactly an unfamiliar feeling, is it?

Mike McCarthy has done a good job leading the Steelers to this point and maintaining a winning culture long held under Tomlin. McCarthy, Brian Angelichio, and the offensive staff have impressed by establishing a bully ball identity and making the most of a failing wide receiver room. Patrick Graham and his staff, notably defensive line coach Domata Peko, seem to be getting the most of a vaunted pass rush and have a top-six unit against both yards and points through eight games.

Especially with the expected growing pains of a new staff and scheme, things have gone about as well as could be hoped from a coaching perspective as we enter November. In some ways, you could argue Pittsburgh looks better right now than it has in recent seasons with the offensive line finally clicking, the best inside linebacker play the team has seen in years, and a lot of young talent sprinkled throughout the roster.

But Steelers fans aren’t new to regular-season success. If McCarthy and co. want to show real improvement over the late-Tomlin era, it will have to be earned through the next several postseasons and the hunt for the team’s first franchise quarterback post-Ben Roethlisberger.

The verdict: So far so good, but it’s too early to be meaningful.

Pittsburgh’s wide receiver room is a problem

RP: The Steelers’ passing attack is not among the league’s best. As a group, they are generating -0.18 EPA per dropback, which is 26th in the NFL. Roman Wilson is the only receiver with more than one touchdown (2), and he’s been out since leaving the game against the Colts in Week 5. DK Metcalf is the team’s leader in both receptions (33) and yards (378), and that comes to an average of 4.1 receptions and 47.3 yards per game through eight games. That’s certainly not good enough from a player who is paid as much as he is and cost a second-round pick to acquire.

Michael Pittman Jr. has also been shelved for the majority of the season, and while he didn’t cost as much to acquire, the Steelers are likely kicking themselves for the extension they immediately handed him to make him a player with cap hits above $26 million and $24 million for the next two seasons.

So yeah, the group has been bad. And yet — I still think we’re overemphasizing it. Metcalf clearly has the yips. The drop that led to the interception was brutal, unquestionably. I’m not sure that will improve this season. But in Metcalf’s defense, his fit with Rodgers was always illogical. Rodgers likes precise route runners, and he also throws a lot of quick game concepts. Neither of those truly fit with Metcalf’s skillset. That doesn’t fully excuse Metcalf’s drops and lack of production, but I do wonder if his lack of success on all of those ill-conceived fade routes has carried over to the rest of his game.

That said, for all Metcalf’s struggles this season, he’s still an aggressive and eager blocker, which is kind of what this team needs with its current identity. We can agree he’s being overpaid if that’s the best quality he’s bringing to this team, but if Rodgers and McCarthy can consider mixing up his usage and lowering his overall volume in the passing game, I’m curious if he might be more efficient in the second half of the season.

Germie Bernard has started three games, and in my opinion, has cemented himself as arguably the best weapon the Steelers have at receiver. When the Steelers prioritized giving him a heavy volume in his first start, he turned 12 catches into 11 receptions for 87 yards and the game-winning score. However, in the following two games he only drew five targets a game.

Part of that is because the Steelers heavily featured the running game against the Saints and Browns — with 27 and 32 running back attempts, respectively — but Rodgers still targeted Metcalf more. Metcalf turned 12 targets into three receptions for 60 yards, with a despicable outing against Cleveland resulting in that interception and just one reception for four yards. Rodgers frequently passed up an open Bernard in both games, but especially against Cleveland. Bernard’s average depth of target was low in both games, 8.0 yards against the Saints and an absurd 0.8 yards against the Browns. Across the two games, he turned his limited opportunities into eight receptions for 57.

Could the Steelers use more help at receiver? Undeniably. But I do think a healthy return of Pittman Jr. and Wilson will help, even if only slightly. But I think the Steelers are best when they are in multi-tight end sets anyway. This team’s identity is best suited for running the ball and then building a passing attack that plays off of that. I don’t think there are many in-season solutions in terms of trades or signings that will drastically flip this offense. At least not with Rodgers holding the reins, I don’t see many dramatic scheme changes coming, though I do believe fewer fade routes to Metcalf and building more around Bernard would net better outcomes moving forward. But if the team leans into its two-tight-end sets, jumbo packages, and running the ball, I do think they can still be competitive.

The verdict: It most definitely is. And yet still not as bad as it’s being made out to be, if the team can just fully embrace what it does well offensively and cut down on the number of low-success-rate plays they refuse to give up on.

Aaron Rodgers caps the Steelers’ ceiling

RB: This is a sizable can of worms and probably not the best fit for your (hopefully) favorite long-winded Steelers column. But like most, whenever I consider the Steelers’ realistic Super Bowl-contending odds, it always comes down to whether or not the team’s quarterback/passing game can rise to the challenge. And I always tend to lean towards “no.”

While obviously no longer in his prime, Rodgers has improved on some of his worst habits from last year, averaging almost an entire yard more in air yards per attempt this season, and increasing his average time to throw from 2.59 to 2.7 seconds (it jumps up to 2.86 seconds without a blitz). Yes, his incompletions and interceptions have jumped up significantly, but that is both a symptom of taking some more risks and having a wide receiver core that occasionally forgets catching is part of the job (see above segment).

Still, Rodgers’ air yards per attempt and time to throw are bottom-10 in the NFL among qualified passers. He’s tied for the fifth-worst EPA per dropback. His obvious preferences for one-on-one fades and checking to throws in the red zone have clearly hurt offensive efficiency. And while he’s largely been more mobile this year, Rodgers still tends to look and play uncomfortably in games where he expects pressure. He can still pick defenses apart from a clean pocket, but highlight plays are few and far between compared with the best passers in the league.

Rodgers’ veteran savvy has clearly helped the Steelers win some close games over his time with the team, with the Steelers’ win-and-in game against the Ravens to end the 2025 regular season standing out as a clear example. Without a doubt, the future Hall of Famer has been a crucial piece of the offense’s high points as of late.

The Steelers’ passing game has been inconsistent at best this season, but with the team’s constant injuries at wide receiver and DK Metcalf having arguably the worst year of his career, it’s hard to heap too much blame on the quarterback. Still, when watching the NFL’s most dangerous contenders in 2026, you tend to see a higher level of play under center.

Of course, the Seahawks won the Super Bowl last year with good-not-elite quarterback play. But among other factors, it also took a complete defense with an elite secondary, along with a knack for explosives in the passing game. I don’t think the Steelers have either.

The verdict: Long story short? Yes. But Rodgers is also a crucial floor-raiser.

No Joey Porter Jr.? No problem.

RP: I went on quite a while earlier about this defense, so I won’t draw this out too much. Credit should go to Patrick Graham for getting the most out of what I consider an imperfect secondary that has also dealt with its fair share of injuries.

Graham is putting players like Ramsey in a position to succeed by highlighting what they do well. In Ramsey’s case, that’s more play around the line of scrimmage and drastically reducing the number of high-stress coverage assignments. Ramsey already has 20 stops, a stat that measures tackles resulting in a negative outcome for the offense. His career single-season high is 27. Through half a season, Ramsey has 34 pass-rushing snaps, just 13 off his career single-season high. Likewise, his 247 snaps from the slot should have him blowing past his previous career high, 353, which he set last year. The difference between last year, though, is that the Steelers are playing more zone and asking Ramsey to cover more tight ends and running backs. He’s no longer the lockdown corner he was in his prime, and Graham isn’t asking him to be, which wasn’t always true under the previous regime.

The rest of the secondary is, so far, proving to be greater than the sum of its parts, though my earlier worry about the talent level of quarterbacks they’ve played remains. The pass defense remains middle of the pack in terms of success rate, and the Steelers have faced few killers under center this season.

Jamel Dean has been awesome thus far, and is the defensive back that gives me the least worries. Asante Samuel Jr. has been a nice surprise, but he’s a cornerback I view as matchup-dependent. Against players with bigger size, like against the Bengals, he can struggle. Rookies Daylen Everette and Robert Spears-Jennings have played well for rookies, but aren’t mistake-free and have yet to be truly tested by a dangerous passer. Jaquan Brisker is an awesome run defender and physical presence over the middle, but I think he’s gettable in coverage, allowing 17 catches on 23 targets.

The verdict: The team would be better with him, but it isn’t entirely lost without him.

The interior defensive line is dominating

RB: I’ve been banging this drum for a while. The Steelers’ edge rusher room has the most big names, but the Steelers’ defensive line has been just as if not even more crucial to the team’s success rushing the passer and stopping the run this season. We knew the depth would be strong here entering this season, but what has been surprising has been the emergence of players such as Gabriel Rubio and Kevin Jobity Jr. while Derrick Harmon and Sebastian Joseph-Day have missed time with injuries.

Like Watt, Cameron Heyward is on track to play a career-low percentage of defensive snaps (63.1%) and has responded with more efficiency: his first double-digit pressure rate since 2022. Playing more 3-tech this season, Keeanu Benton has arrived and is on track for a career-high 38 stops with 18 through eight games. Yahya Black (13) and Rubio (six) have combined for 19 stops, living up to their pre-draft billings as run-stuffers. And despite a smaller sample size (23 defensive snaps) Jobity has the third-highest pressure rate of the group (10%).

Once Harmon comes back, this group should get even stronger. Before his injury, Harmon had more than doubled his rookie-year pressure rate (5.7% to 14.3%) — he was already a competent run stuffer in 2025, and now things are starting to click as a rusher.

The emergence of Benton is the biggest story here (I wrote about that earlier this season here), but it’s been the mix of him, the star power of Heyward, and a long list of capable depth lineman that have arguably been the biggest part of the Steelers’ defensive success this season. Don’t underrate this group.

The verdict: Yes.

It’s time to be a little worried about Chris Boswell

RP: Boswell is 16-for-16 on extra point attempts this year. He’s 18-for-18 on field goals from within 47 yards. His misses this year came from: 56, 57, 48, 48, and 57. He hasn’t missed more than once in any game. It’s not like he’s missed any gimmes, and he hasn’t spiraled and had a second one when he has had a miss in a game. What are we doing here?

The verdict: Shut up. Don’t be stupid.

Jaylen Warren for Offensive Player of the Year?

RB: As a long-time Warren believer, it’s been funny watching the online narrative change from “Maybe Jaylen Warren should start over Najee Harris/Kenneth Gainwell” to “He might be one of the best offensive players in the NFL this year.”

That said, the Warren for Offensive Player of the Year campaign isn’t as far-fetched as you might think given that he’s currently sixth in the NFL in rushing yards (704, just 76 behind first), first among qualified runners in yards per carry (5.9), tied for second in 20-plus-yard runs (seven) and second in receiving yards among running backs (245, still 94 behind leader Ashton Jeanty). He’s also third in the entire league in yards from scrimmage (998), not far behind Jaxon Smith-Njigba (1,014) and Jahmyr Gibbs (1,058).

Warren has made highlight plays, he’s on a winning team, and he’s undoubtedly been the engine of Pittsburgh’s offense to start the season. At this rate, he should be one of the top names for the award. But I still think he’s a ways away from being a front-runner.

For one, Warren’s touchdown production (just three total rushing and receiving) lags far behind the leaders of the pack with Pittsburgh repeatedly not running enough in the red zone. His volume is also not incredibly high (13th-most touches among running backs) and could continue to drop as the Steelers keep rotating in a now-healthy Rico Dowdle. Beyond that, Warren lacks the name recognition of household stars such as Smith-Njigba (on track for the first 2,000-yard receiving season), Gibbs, and even Kenneth Walker III, whose play has helped put the Chiefs back in contender status. The latter two are also on track for 1,800-yard-plus rushing seasons. (It’s worth noting a quarterback hasn’t won this award since 2018).

If that feels like fantasy football logic, you’re not wrong, but that’s just how NFL awards work. Frankly, I wouldn’t get my hopes up too high with this narrative, but it is worth noting just how remarkable Warren has been so far this season — the first offensive superstar the Steelers have had since arguably the Killer B era. At the very least, Warren is definitely in the OPOY conversation, which is impressive in and of itself considering no Steeler has ever won the award.

The verdict: Probably not, but I’m not going to argue.

The Steelers are Super Bowl contenders

RP: Weirdly, the AFC playoff picture seems all but set save for seeding. Barring the Browns and Raiders proving they’re legitimate, the 4-5 Ravens surviving without Lamar Jackson and Jacoby Brissett at the helm, and/or a miracle turn by the 2-5 Texans, the remaining AFC field outside of the playoffs presently has two or fewer wins.

I mentioned earlier I’d dive more into the quarterbacks, and now the moment is here. If we include some of the bubble teams I mentioned, here are the potential quarterback matchups the Steelers might have, in order of current seeding:

  • Josh Allen (1st in EPA/DB)
  • Bo Nix (20th)
  • Trevor Lawrence (4th)
  • Patrick Mahomes (11th)
  • Joe Burrow (6th)
  • Drake Maye (8th)
  • Deshaun Watson (24th)
  • Kirk Cousins (7th)/Fernando Mendoza (N/A)
  • Jacoby Brissett(23rd)/Tyler Huntley (35th)
  • C.J. Stroud (10th)

Looking at that field, I think the most telling regular-season games on the Steelers’ schedule will come against the Jaguars and the Texans. If the Steelers’ secondary can hold against the Jaguars, I’ll be much more confident in them. A good showing against the Texans would also come against a top-10 quarterback in EPA per dropback this season, and a team win might contribute to keeping the Texans out of the playoffs all together.

Right now, I would not be confident against the Bills or the Jaguars.

I could talk myself into close game wins against the Broncos and Chiefs, though I’d be nervous the whole game. I am not scared of Denver’s offense, and they’re actually a pretty bad run defense this year (third-worst EPA allowed per rush, eighth most rushing yards allowed per game), but if the Steelers stubbornly go pass-heavy as they’ve been prone to with Rodgers, it could get ugly. Likewise, the Chiefs offense doesn’t really scare me unless they add a dynamic pass catcher before the deadline, but their defense is good, and Patrick Mahomes is about as good as there is at winning ugly games. A close game late would have to favor Kansas City in most scenarios.

I’m slightly less afraid of the Patriots and Bengals, both of whom I think are beatable, but I acknowledge the Steelers could also lose to them on any given Sunday. The Bengals are a rival with the type of offense to give Pittsburgh trouble, and the Patriots have a decent defense and the type of quarterback who can make enough plays to gut out a win if the Steelers offense doesn’t show up to play.

The Texans might miss entirely, and I will wait and see how the regular season matchup goes. The defense has not performed on the same level it did a year ago, though it still remains dangerous if it hits its stride — which, if they make the playoffs after starting 2-5, you have to imagine it would have.

I like the Steelers’ chances against a Lamar-less Ravens squad; we’ll see if they hang in the race. The Raiders and Browns are both teams the Steelers should beat.

The verdict: I’m more confident they can win a playoff game than I have been since the 2017 season. But a Super Bowl appearance, let alone a win, still seems far-fetched.

item.title: Falcons list James Pearce, Divine Diablo as questionable for Sunday
item.description: Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich said this week that the Falcons plan to use linebacker James Pearce in a pass rushing role against the Bengals in Madrid this Sunday, but the team didn't guarantee he'll be playing on their final injury report of the week.
item.content:encoded:
Falcons defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich said this week that the Falcons plan to use linebacker James Pearce in a pass rushing role against the Bengals in Madrid this Sunday, but the team didn't guarantee he'll be playing on their final injury report of the week.

Pearce is listed as questionable to play in his first week back from an eight-game suspension. Pearce was a full participant in practice this week and was not dealing with any injury earlier in the week, but the team listed him with a back issue on Friday. They will have to formally add him to the active roster in order for him to be in the lineup in Week 9.

The Falcons also listed linebacker Divine Deablo (forearm) as questionable to return after missing the last two games. Deablo was also a full participant in practice.

Linebacker Yasir Abdullah (hamstring), defensive back Billy Bowman (hamstring), wide receiver Beaux Collins (hip), and offensive tackle Cameron Williams (ankle) are also listed as questionable after full practice participation.

Wide receiver Zachariah Branch (hamstring) was ruled out earlier this week and did not travel to Spain. Running back Brian Robinson (hamstring) was ruled out on Friday.

item.title: 5 things to watch as Jets face Chiefs in Week 8 of 2026 NFL season
item.description: The Jets will be heavy underdogs in their visit to face the Kansas City Chiefs.
item.content:encoded:
The Jets have fallen to 2-6 on the season and will be looking back on the last few games with regret as matchups they will feel they should have won. 

It’s a different proposition this week, though, as they will be heavy underdogs in their visit to face the Kansas City Chiefs.

Let’s review the top storylines to watch as the Jets look to pull off the upset...

A get-right game for the Chiefs

The Chiefs got off to a 5-0 start but have since lost their last two. Clearly, they’ll be expecting to halt that slide on Sunday.

Unfortunately for New York, the two-game losing streak makes it unlikely the Chiefs overlook them. It will be a good measuring stick for the Jets, who have suffered five of their six losses this season in one-score games.

How will the Jets stop the run?

Defensive linemen David Onyemata and T’Vondre Sweat are already on IR, and now Harrison Phillips has an injury concern after an ankle issue kept him out of practice on Wednesday. If Phillips is unable to play on Sunday, the Jets will be without all three of their starting linemen.

That bodes well for the Chiefs, who have the No. 5 rushing game in the NFL. Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker, who was signed during the offseason, is just 10 yards off the league lead with 770.

Last Sunday, to their credit, the Jets did quite well against the run, as they held the Raiders below three yards per carry. Backups Darrell Jackson Jr., Jowon Briggs and Jack Heflin will need to continue to hold their own, even if Phillips suits up.

Can the Jets get everyone involved on offense?

It’s been a long time since the Jets had as many offensive weapons at their disposal as they do right now. However, they are still striving for the right balance in terms of getting everyone involved.

Last week saw New York make an effort to involve Garrett Wilson more, and featured a career-high 142-yard game from AD Mitchell, who had gone without a catch in the previous game. However, Omar Cooper Jr. wasn’t targeted at all coming off back-to-back 100-yard games and the team drew criticism for abandoning the running game in the second half.

This has been an issue all year. After a breakout 100-yard game against the Lions, rookie tight end Kenyon Sadiq has just five catches for 43 yards in the past five weeks. In addition, Jeremy Ruckert – who had a career-high five catches and a touchdown in the same game – hasn’t been targeted at all since then.

Will New York’s special teams unit reverse its fortune?

Having been outstanding in 2025, the Jets’ special teams unit has been poor in 2026, and it let them down again on Sunday when Dylan Laube returned a kickoff for a 95-yard touchdown. Can Chris Banjo’s unit use this game to get back to the kind of impact they were making last season?

One area where the Jets might have the edge is in the kicking game, because the usually stellar Harrison Butker has really been struggling. Butker has missed six field goals, and his 67 percent success rate this season is easily the lowest of his career. Butker will be feeling the pressure to be flawless on Sunday after the Chiefs recently added Justin Tucker to their practice squad as competition for him.

The interception drought lives on

Back in Week 4, Minkah Fitzpatrick’s interception of Tyson Bagent snapped New York’s incredible streak of 21 games without an interception. In addition, they intercepted another three passes that day, although each of those was negated by a penalty. Nevertheless, it seemed like a strong sign that this year’s team would be much better at making plays on the ball.

Since then, however, four games have passed and the Jets have failed to intercept a pass in any of them. Including Fitzpatrick’s interception, the Jets have just one in 25 games under Glenn, as that play is starting to look more like an aberration than a sign this would start becoming a more regular occurrence.

item.title: 5 things to watch as Giants face Eagles in Week 9 of 2026 NFL season
item.description: Here are the main storylines to watch as the Giants face the Eagles in Week 9 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
The Giants haven’t won in Philadelphia since 2013, but this could be their big chance as the Eagles are having a rough year. They are 2-6 and reeling after quarterback Jalen Hurts was ruled out for the rest of the season due to blood clots. On Sunday, they’ll be looking to avoid a seventh straight loss.

Let’s review the top storylines to watch as the Giants continue their quest for the NFC East crown...

Joe Milton’s first career start

With Hurts out, the Giants probably expected to face Tanner McKee, a player who beat them in the 2024 season finale when he passed for 269 yards and two scores. 

McKee was the subject of trade buzz during the offseason, with the suggestion being that some teams were looking at him as a potential starter. However, once he got his shot with the Eagles, he underwhelmed, losing three starts in a row and failing to exceed 215 passing yards in any of them.

Philadelphia has opted to make a change and give Milton a shot after acquiring the strong-armed former Patriots and Cowboys passer a few weeks ago. Although he has never started a game, Milton passed for 241 yards off the bench in last year’s season finale with New England, so the Giants at least have some pro film of him to get a sense of what he brings to the table.

A running game in flux

New York’s running backs came up big in their last game, the overtime win against the Texans in Houston. Four different players rushed for a touchdown, including Devin Singletary’s walk-off game winner. However, as rumors of potential interest in a trade for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor circulate, the running game situation is unclear.

The Giants recently released Najee Harris and may wish they hadn’t, because Tyrone Tracy Jr. has since landed on IR. In addition, Cam Skattebo, who rushed for over 100 yards against the Texans, is dealing with a hamstring issue and could be a game-time decision. This would leave Singletary under pressure to deliver, with some inexperienced players behind him on the bench.

Deonte Banks continues to prove himself

Considered by many a long-shot to even make the roster this season, Banks is finally living up to his draft position.

Banks, who won an NFL Defensive Player of the Week Award last month, furthered his renewed reputation in the Texans game by impressively holding Nico Collins to just two catches for six yards.

New York just signed Greg Newsome II to a three-year extension, and Banks reportedly rejected a similar deal at the same time. He will no doubt want to prove he’s worth more than Newsome and should have a good chance to do that.

With A.J. Brown now in New England and DeVonta Smith nursing a hamstring injury, rookie Makai Lemon leads the Eagles with 31 receptions, but he’s only averaging 8.1 yards per catch.

What does Saquon Barkley have left in the tank?

Barkley has been dealing with some injury issues of his own, which have seen him limited in recent weeks. He has rushed for just 100 yards total since Week 3 and hasn’t been a weapon in the passing game all year, with just seven catches for 41 yards.

New York shouldn’t overlook him, though. Barkley is still averaging almost five yards per carry and is usually motivated to do well against his former team, with 150 and 176 yard games on the ground against them over the past two seasons.

Can Dominic Zvada repay John Harbaugh's confidence in him?

Harbaugh stated that he has full confidence in Zvada this week, despite the fact that Zvada has missed five field goals in his past three games.

Zvada, who was undrafted out of Michigan, started the season well by making all 14 of his kicks in the first four games. However, he’s been regularly missing field goals in close games since then and will be feeling the pressure on Sunday.

item.title: Three reasons the Jaguars beat the Ravens
item.description: Three key aspects of the Jaguars’ brutal dismantling of the Ravens on Thursday night:
item.content:encoded:
The Jacksonville Jaguars continued their impressive 2026 campaign on Thursday night, dismantling the Baltimore Ravens 33-10 at M&T Bank Stadium. In a game played through torrential rain, Trevor Lawrence and the offense did enough to put points on the board, but it was another outstanding defensive performance that ultimately made the difference.

Jacksonville improved to 6-2, extending its lead at the top of the AFC South, while Baltimore suffered a fourth consecutive defeat. There were plenty of reasons for optimism in another convincing Jaguars victory, but these three stood out.

The defense made life miserable for Baltimore

Jacksonville’s defense has quietly become one of the most reliable units in the NFL, and Thursday night provided another demonstration of just how good this group can be.

The Jaguars entered Week 9 ranked second in the NFL in points allowed, and they backed that reputation up by limiting Baltimore to just 227 total yards, 10 first downs and 10 points. The Ravens converted just four of their 14 third-down opportunities, while Jacksonville forced three turnovers, including interceptions by Montaric Brown and Jourdan Lewis.

Brown’s interception came on Baltimore’s opening possession of the second half, immediately putting the Jaguars in position to extend their lead. Lewis provided another takeaway in the fourth quarter, with both interceptions ultimately helping Jacksonville add field goals.

There was also an important battle in the trenches. Despite losing defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton for the season earlier in the week, Jacksonville restricted Derrick Henry to just 57 yards on 17 carries. That’s an average of 3.4 yards per attempt against one of the most productive running backs of his generation.

Admittedly, Justice Hill’s 65-yard touchdown run late in the fourth quarter took some of the shine off the final defensive numbers. However, until that point, Baltimore had managed just three points on its opening drive before going scoreless across its next nine offensive possessions.

The Ravens were missing Lamar Jackson and Tyler Huntley, but that shouldn’t detract from the execution. Jacksonville did exactly what a good defense should do against a struggling offense: create pressure, take the football away and prevent the opposition from building any momentum.

This was another performance that suggests the Jaguars’ defense can be a genuine strength as the season progresses.

Trevor Lawrence delivered the defining moment

Trevor Lawrence didn’t need to put together a spectacular statistical performance to make his mark on this game. Instead, he delivered when Jacksonville needed him most.

The quarterback completed 16 of 26 passes for 242 yards and a touchdown, finishing with a 105.0 passer rating and spreading the football around eight different receivers.

His most important contribution came just before halftime. With the Jaguars holding a narrow 10-3 advantage, Lawrence led a four-play, 80-yard scoring drive that completely changed the complexion of the contest. The highlight was a beautifully executed 50-yard touchdown connection with Parker Washington, who beat his defender and found plenty of space behind the Baltimore secondary.

It was a significant moment. Jacksonville went into the locker room with a 17-3 lead rather than allowing the Ravens an opportunity to remain within one score and potentially build some momentum after the break.

Lawrence was particularly effective attacking downfield. According to Next Gen Stats, he completed eight of 10 passes travelling at least 10 air yards, accumulating 193 yards and a touchdown on those attempts. His 80% completion rate on downfield throws was his second-best mark of the season.

That’s an encouraging development for a quarterback who has increasingly looked comfortable leading this offense.

There was no need for Lawrence to chase huge numbers in the second half. Jacksonville had established control, and he managed the game effectively while allowing the defense and special teams to do their jobs.

The Jaguars are becoming increasingly difficult to beat when their quarterback can produce big plays without needing to force the issue.

Jacksonville won the battle of complementary football

Perhaps the most encouraging aspect of this victory was how effectively Jacksonville’s different units worked together.

This wasn’t a game in which Lawrence needed to throw for 350 yards or the defense needed to score a touchdown to rescue the offense. Instead, the Jaguars consistently put themselves in advantageous positions and took the opportunities presented to them.

Their opening drive was an excellent example. Lawrence connected with tight end Nate Boerkircher for a 52-yard gain on the second play from scrimmage, setting up Bhayshul Tuten’s one-yard touchdown run to give Jacksonville an early advantage.

The offense continued to find ways to move the football, while Cam Little converted all four of his field-goal attempts. Jacksonville finished with 319 total yards, averaging 5.7 yards per play, and produced seven scoring drives.

Importantly, the defense repeatedly helped the offense maintain control. Brown’s interception set up a field goal early in the second half, while Lewis’ fourth-quarter pick provided another short field. A fumble recovery by linebacker Jalen McLeod following the ensuing kickoff also helped Jacksonville put the game beyond doubt, with Chris Rodriguez Jr. eventually powering in from two yards out to make it 33-3.

It was a thoroughly professional performance in difficult conditions. The rain made life challenging for both offenses, but Jacksonville avoided the costly mistakes that could have allowed Baltimore back into the contest.

The Jaguars didn’t need to dominate one particular statistical category to win. They simply executed their assignments, capitalized on mistakes and made sure the Ravens had very few opportunities to change the game’s direction.

That’s the kind of football that wins games in November and December.

The verdict

There will be tougher tests ahead, and Jacksonville will need to maintain this level of performance against healthier and more dangerous opponents. However, back-to-back victories over the Indianapolis Colts and Baltimore Ravens have provided plenty of evidence that this team deserves to be taken seriously.

Lawrence is playing some of the best football of his career, the defense is consistently producing results, and the supporting cast is doing its part.

At 6-2, the Jaguars are building a significant cushion in the AFC South. More importantly, they’re beginning to look like a team capable of making some serious noise when the postseason arrives.

item.title: An All-22 look inside the blitzing arsenal of Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores
item.description: A film session to the blitz packages of Vikings DC Brian Flores
item.content:encoded:
A game against the Vikings means your offense will get the full Brian Flores Experience, a blitz-crazed defense that sends two or three extra rushers at your offensive line…all game.

That’s what the Buffalo Bills have in front of them on Monday Night Football in Week 9. Entering this contest, Minnesota owns the league’s highest blitz rate (on dropbacks) at 74.2%. The Commanders are second at 44.5%, and the league average is 31.2%. Minnesota blitzes frequently on run plays too.

Let’s dig into the ingenuity of Flores’ enormous blitzing arsenal.

We’ll begin in Week 1, Minnesota’s game against Jordan Love and the Packers.

What you’ll see below is Vikings in an overload look to the left side of the Packers offensive front… with four defenders on the line of scrimmage on that side of the ball, compared to just two on the other side of the center.

But at the snap is when the calculated chaos ensued.

Cornerback Byron Murphy, who initially looked to be covering Christian Watson in a tight split near the numbers on the upper portion of the screen, screamed off the edge as a blitzer.

Meanwhile, on the other side of the defensive front, Andrew Van Ginkel, floated backward into coverage, and cornerback Isaiah Rodgers is actually the furthest outside blitzer.

With the all the down linemen sliding left, it provided Rodgers a free run into the backfield:

Watch again, and notice how the Packers tight end Josh Whyle — originally in motion —was ready for Rodgers and picked him up as he cut back toward the left side of Green Bay’s line.

However, because his blocking assignment drew him in that direction, he wasn’t positioned to help the right side of the Packers front that suddenly featured a right tackle stretched exceptionally wide by Murphy’s cornerback blitz and Minnesota’s most purely gifted outside rusher Dallas Turner erupting past the right guard.

Even when an offensive line thinks it picks up the blitzer Flores intended to get a free run, there’s often a secondary hole opened for another defender to disrupt the pocket.

Flores absolutely will show all-out, eight-man pressure in this game. It’s one of his trademarks. That doesn’t always mean eight defenders are entering the rush on that play. In fact, that rarely happens. Discerning which defender(s) will drop into coverage is the challenge, particularly as the game clock is winding down.

Like here, against the Packers, the Vikings showed an eight-pass pressure package. Behind that hyper-aggressive look was plenty of green grass before three defensive backs roughly 10 yards beyond the line of scrimmage, splitting the field into thirds.

Pay close attention to what transpired at the snap and a split second later. The two outer most rushers on the left side of their defensive front show blitz but never actually rushed the quarterback, and linebacker Blake Cashman dropped into coverage underneath. On the edge, Van Ginkel watched the quarterback and kept contain.

Jordan Love missed a wide-open out-breaking route at the 40 yard line because he’s forced into a quick decision which ultimately was a deep-ball attempt toward Christian Watson that was nearly intercepted.

The takeaway from that blitz is critical. Quite naturally, the Vikings have to drop at least one defender toward the side of the field with more receivers.

That feature of Minnesota’s blitzes is noteworthy. It’s the one distinct way an offense’s pass game can dictate to the Vikings defense.

Note here, on this blitz against the Buccaneers, how linebacker Eric Wilson sunk at the snap toward the side of the field with three receivers for Tampa Bay.

And, sometimes, the sinking defender (occasionally it’s two defenders) take three or four steps to sell blitz before retreating into a short zone.

Like here against the Lions.

There are two receivers to Jared Goff’s right in this pre-snap alignment. At the snap, and even a second after it, the Vikings made a convincing case for an an all-out, eight-man pressure. But the blitz only featured seven, as Cashman exploded forward, disappeared into the middle of Detroit’s offensive line then dropped into the middle of the field to take away Jahmyr Gibbs’ underneath route.

In those all-out blitz looks, even if the Vikings ultimately send six or seven rushers — which is still an extremely high amount of rushers toward the quarterback — it’s beneficial for the offense to feature as many routes with quick breaks off the vertical stem as possible.

On that specific play, notice how Jameson Williams and Amon Ra-St. Brown ran vertically and didn’t have their heads fully turned around as Goff was being sacked.

Sure, the Lions were in a seven-man protection, but the offense can’t assume every blocker will find his exact assignment in a flash after the snap.

And I’ve saved the most creative Flores blitz for last.

This came on a sack of Daniel Jones against the Colts.

Rather unusually, the Vikings were clearly in man coverage across the board — they’ve used man just 7.2% of the time, the lowest rate in the league and well below the NFL average of 22.4%. And it wasn’t an all-out pressure look, as it was reasonably easy to discern Minnesota’s five “known rushers” before the snap.

But pay close attention to the defender second-furthest from the left edge along Minnesota’s front. It’s Cashman, and at the snap, he started toward the Colts right tackle, as if he was going to deploy a stunt with edge rusher Dallas Turner. After selling the DT-DE stunt — Cash was effectively a defensive tackle on that play — he planted his foot in the ground to change directions completely and loop all the way through the A gap.

Unsurprisingly Cashman got a free run at Jones and registered the sack.

I don’t believe I’ve ever seen that type of blitz before. That’s not to say it’s the first of its kind in NFL history, yet that type of creativity with one defender is exceptionally rare.

So now… got all that?

Imagine an entire offensive line group, extra blocking help in the backfield, and the quarterback processing everything in front of them in roughly 10-15 seconds after breaking the huddle and then again in one second after the snap.

It’s precisely what makes facing this Flores defense so difficult.

Offenses know they’re going to blitz on almost every snap.

But the Vikings don’t care if they’re predictable because they have such a wide variety of blitzes to stress the offensive communication throughout the duration of each contest.

item.title: Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins preview, prediction: On Paper
item.description: A statistical breakdown, preview and predictions for Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions are beat up after a physical and emotional win over the Minnesota Vikings. And while they must travel to play a 1-6 Miami Dolphins team, they can’t afford to underestimate them. The NFC North is too competitive for a trap game, and the Dolphins are a little scrappier than they appear.

But is there a real chance of an upset in Miami, or are the Lions clearly the better team? Let’s examine it in our Lions vs. Dolphins preview and prediction. It’s time for On Paper.

Lions pass offense (8th in DVOA) vs. Dolphins pass defense (29th)

The Lions’ passing offense remains one of their most reliable units on the team. While last week’s performance against the Vikings wasn’t explosive, it was certainly a lot better than most teams manage against Minnesota’s defense. While the DVOA ranking remains outside the top five, I still believe Detroit’s passing attack should be in that top tier.

For the season, they rank:

  • Fourth in passer rating (110.0)
  • Seventh in yards per attempt (7.9)
  • Third in dropback EPA (0.264)
    • First in EPA/pass (+0.21)
  • Fourth in dropback success rate (51.4%)

Detroit is humming in all facets of their passing attack. In pass protection, the Lions allow the fifth-lowest pressure percentage (30.1%), rank seventh in pass-block win rate (54%), and rank third in PFF team pass-blocking grade (75.1).

The Dolphins may have a worse pass defense than the Lions. Five out of the seven quarterbacks who have faced Miami have finished with a passer rating of 119.8 or higher. Granted, they’ve played some really good quarterbacks in Brock Purdy, Patrick Mahomes, Joe Burrow, and Drake Maye. Still, those quarterbacks have outperformed their year-long efficiency against Miami, and the DVOA ranking—which adjusts to opponents’ strength—proves this is a bad pass defense.

Overall, they rank:

  • 32nd in passer rating allowed (119.5)
  • 32nd in yards per attempt (8.3)
  • 32nd in dropback EPA (0.288)
  • 32nd in dropback success rate (53.7%)

This is the result of having an extremely young and inexperienced back seven.

Though there is some recent hope for Miami’s pass rush. As Erik Schlitt pointed out in his Honolulu Blueprint, while the season-long stats don’t look great for the Dolphins’ ability to get to the passer (35.6% pressure rate, 18th; 4.2% sack rate, 28th), they’ve started to put things together. All nine of their sacks have come in the last four games, and they’ve posted a pressure rate of 39.5% or higher in three out of four of those games (league average is around 36%).

Over those last four games, the Dolphins’ pass defense has been better, but certainly not good. From Weeks 4-8, Miami ranks 27th in dropback EPA (0.180) and 29th in success rate (50.7%).

Player to watch: Sam LaPorta. It’s been a quiet few weeks for the Lions tight end, but Miami is allowing the sixth-highest yardage to tight ends (483 yards) and tied for the fourth-most touchdowns (six).

Advantage: Lions +3. This is a top-five unit vs. a bottom-five unit. The only reason I’m not giving it a higher advantage is that some things are trending Miami’s way, and weather could also play a factor, with some slight chance of rain.

Lions run offense (4th) vs. Dolphins run defense (26th)

The Lions’ rushing attack still has frustrating bouts of inconsistency, but last week’s performance against the Vikings felt like a revelation. Whether Detroit’s sidecar formation was a Vikings-specific answer or the cracking of the code for the entire season, we’ll see. But it shows one thing for certain: Lions offensive coordinator Drew Petzing is capable of finding some answers.

For the season, the Lions rushing attack now ranks:

  • Ninth in yards per carry (4.6)
  • 13th in rush EPA (-0.083)
  • Third in success rate (47.0%)

But I must continue to repeat myself that the negative plays are a big problem. The Lions’ 19.3% stuffed rate is sixth in the NFL. Those figures are down from last week (20.9%, third-highest), but it still remains an issue to track. Detroit’s power success rank also improved after last week, but they still rank just 24th, converting on just 59% of short-yardage situations.

Still, it’s worth pointing out how both the offensive line and the running backs are doing their parts. Detroit’s line ranks third in adjusted line yards, eighth in run block win rate, and fourth in PFF run blocking grade. Meanwhile, Detroit’s backfield ranks sixth in rushing yards over expected per rush (+0.5), sixth in yards after contact per rush (3.38), and Jahmyr Gibbs ranks fourth in missed tackle forced rate (31.9%).

This chart doesn’t exactly vibe with the Dolphins’ bottom-10 DVOA ranking. They’re not giving up a ton of yards nor a ton of yards per carry. So what gives? Let’s look deeper.

  • Eighth in yards per carry allowed (3.8)
  • 22nd in rush EPA (-0.078)
  • 30th in rush success rate (43.9%)

In short, it appears the Dolphins don’t give up a ton of big, explosive plays, but they essentially give up exactly what the offense needs. That’s backed by data. Miami has only given up 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th), and just three rushes of 20+ yards (t-sixth fewest).

The good news is the Dolphins are weak where the Lions’ run offense struggles. They’ve produced just a 14.9% stuffed rate (23rd), and they rank 21st in power success rate, allowing conversions on 68% of short-yardage situations.

Player to watch: Jacob Rodriguez. The Dolphins rookie linebacker has been a fun player to watch thus far. Rodriguez has been credited with 30 “stops” per PFF (plays that are a failure for offense), which is second most among ALL NFL linebackers, not just rookies. Seventeen of those have come in the run, t-eighth most.

Advantage: Lions +1.5. I’m not sure I’d expect a huge game from Gibbs and company, given that Miami has not allowed over 150 rushing yards in a game. But Detroit should be fairly efficient on the ground.

Dolphins pass offense (26th) vs. Lions pass defense (24th)

It hasn’t been a great start to the year for Malik Willis in his new home, but it’s hard to blame him given the supporting cast. He’s got an extremely young receiving corps, a new offensive system, and an imbalanced offensive line. As a result, the Dolphins rank:

  • 26th in passer rating (79.7)
  • 20th in yards per attempt (6.9)
  • 23rd in dropback EPA (0.014)
  • 20th in dropback success rate (43.8%)

The Dolphins aren’t a complete disaster, but they’re clearly below average.

That said, there are some very interesting advanced statistics surrounding Willis. For one, he’s not afraid to chuck it deep. He currently owns the third-highest average depth of target (9.2), and his deep ball percentage of 16.4% ranks first in the NFL (yes, above Jordan Love, too). But he also ranks third in time to throw (3.05), suggesting he likely holds onto the ball too long—especially when you consider the Dolphins have the second-highest sack rate (10.3%).

The offensive line is a mixed bag. Though they’ve allowed the second-highest pressure rate (43.2%), they rank 20th in pass block win rate and 31st in PFF pass blocking grade. The issue is that the left side of their offensive line is good-to-great (LT Patrick Paul is 14th in pass blocking grade, rookie LG Kadyn Proctor is improving) and the right side is a disaster (RT Austin Jackson is dead last in pass blocking grade, RG Jonah Savaiinaea is 63rd out of 76).

And as mentioned before, the receiving corps is ridiculously young: Malik Washington is 25; Caleb Douglas is 23, and Chris Bell is 22. Young doesn’t mean bad, but it’ll take them some time to get adjusted to the NFL.

Is the Lions’ pass defense actually getting better? It’s hard for me to tell. The raw numbers are improving, but as the chart above shows, they’ve also played some pretty bad passing offenses in the last few weeks. I’m not yet convinced.

Overall, the Lions rank:

  • 26th in passer rating allowed (101.0)
  • 18th in yards per attempt (7.3)
  • 29th in dropback EPA (0.218)
  • 28th in success rate (50.0%)

I think it’s also worth noting that the Lions’ pass rush has fallen off a bit as of late. After three weeks, the Lions ranked 10th in pressure rate (39.0%) and second in time to pressure (2.46). The Lions now rank just 17th in pressure rate (35.8%) and 20th in time to pressure (2.68). And this week, they’re almost certainly without DJ Wonnum, who was fourth on the team in pressures (14). That said, the Lions still do rank third in pass rush win rate, third in PFF pass rush grade, and seventh in sack rate. I just worry it’s trending in the wrong direction.

Then, of course, there are the injuries to account for. While it looks like Brian Branch is on track to play, the Lions don’t have MIKE linebacker Jack Campbell, and top cornerback D.J. Reed is trending toward missing this game. Detroit’s back seven has already struggled immensely in coverage, and now they’ll be tested further.

Player to watch: Malik Washington. Washington leads the Dolphins in catches (31) and yards (329), and the Dolphins like to use him all over the field—as a screen weapon or downfield. His 4.47 speed is a weapon.

Advantage: Draw. I’m not particularly impressed with either unit. I think it’s certainly possible Willis hits on a few big downfield plays, and I think it’s also very possible Detroit is able to disrupt and sack Willis 4-6 times this game. In the end, I think it’ll all even out.

Dolphins run offense (26th) vs. Lions run defense (23rd)

This is another weird statistical oddity for Miami. By the charts, it looks like they actually have a good thing going with their run game, including a breakout season from Ollie Gordon (408 yards, 4.5 YPC, 4 TDs) and some quarterback rushing potential from Malik Willis (225 yards, 3 TDs). Yet, the advanced statistics aren’t as impressive. They rank:

  • 11th in yards per carry (4.4)
  • 21st in rush EPA (-0.128)
  • 24th in success rate (36.0%)

It turns out this rushing attack is very boom or bust—like a less-efficient version of Detroit’s running game. They have produced t-sixth-most rushes of 10+ yards (26), but also a 19.1% stuff rate—seventh-highest.

The problem appears to be that the offensive line isn’t carrying their end of the bargain. They rank 26th in run block win rate, 27th in PFF run blocking grade, and 27th in adjusted line yards.

But credit to Gordon for doing everything he can to get the most out of his situation.

I don’t know, man. The Lions are just too inconsistent in the run game this year. They’ve been better lately, but it seems like they’re still susceptible to explosive plays. Overall, the Lions rank:

  • 16th in yards per carry allowed (4.1)
  • 17th in rush EPA (-0.096)
  • 11th in success rate (37.2%)

So that pretty much matches my eye test. They’re decent down-to-down, but they give up too many explosives. Though they’ve only allowed 21 rushes of 10+ yards (t-14th fewest), they’ve allowed six of 20+ yards (t-ninth most).

And with the loss of Jack Campbell, it’s hard to know how this unit will respond. Detroit has an experienced linebacking corps in Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske, but none provide the instincts and consistency of Campbell.

Player to watch: Tyleik Williams. I pointed it out in my Dolphins vs. Patriots thoughts, but Miami really struggled against New England’s nose tackle last week, and Williams remains an impossible guy to move.

Advantage: Dolphins +1. I’m giving Miami a slight advantage here for a couple of reasons. First, I am concerned about the loss of Jack Campbell, and it may take a couple of weeks for Detroit to find a plan that works without him. Second, I do think Willis provides a legitimate rushing threat, and Detroit has lost contain far too often this year. Third, I just think Miami is better than their stats suggest, and the Lions may be a tad worse. It shouldn’t be a dominant day for Miami—and if Detroit can get out to a big lead, they can erase this advantage completely—but I still think Miami has the slight edge here.

Last week’s prediction:

On Paper drops to 5-2 overall and 3-4 against the spread, but I don’t feel all that bad for how my Lions vs. Vikings preview played out. The only area I made a clear mistake was underestimating the Lions’ run game, and for the first half of that game, I looked right. But Petzing made a lot of believers on Sunday, and I’m one of them.

In the comment section, we nearly had two perfect predictions, despite the odd score. Muddy.D’s 19-16 Lions prediction was just a single point away, as was Devil Barrel’s 18-15 Lions prediction. Here is your prize. Share it, or I’ll take it back, and you get nothing.

It’s a football lasso. Just in case you happen to commit the awful sin of spinning a football near an opponent, you can rope it back in before any ref sees!

This week’s prediction:

The Lions come out with a pretty definitive +3.5 advantage. I know the Dolphins have kept it close with some recent opponents, but I’m not really buying it. There isn’t a single thing they do particularly well, and their worst unit (pass defense) happens to match up with Detroit’s best unit (pass offense). I think that could spell disaster for Miami, as they don’t want Malik Willis dropping back 50 times to try and keep pace with Jared Goff.

I think we get our first comfortable Lions win since the Cardinals game. Lions 38, Dolphins 24.
